units.name: Computing Basics & Binary

concepts.intro: A computer is a machine that stores and manipulates data as electrical signals, following a stored program of instructions.
b: The CPU (central processing unit) fetches, decodes, and executes instructions one step at a time
RAM (memory) holds the program and data currently in use; it is fast but erased when power is lost
Storage (SSD/hard drive) holds data permanently, even without power
Input devices (keyboard, mouse, sensors) bring data in; output devices (screen, speaker) send results out
The fetch-decode-execute cycle repeats billions of times per second, measured in Hertz (clock speed)

concepts.intro: Computers represent all data using binary (base-2), a number system with only two digits: 0 and 1, because transistors are easiest to build as simple on/off switches.
b: A single binary digit (0 or 1) is called a bit
8 bits grouped together form a byte, the basic unit of storage (e.g., one character)
Each bit position represents a power of 2: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128...
To convert binary to decimal, add the powers of 2 where there is a 1 (e.g., 1011 = 8+0+2+1 = 11)
To convert decimal to binary, repeatedly divide by 2 and record the remainders
Everything digital — text, images, sound, video — is ultimately stored as sequences of bits

concepts.intro: Hexadecimal (base-16) is a compact way to represent binary values, since each hex digit maps exactly to 4 bits.
b: Hex uses digits 0-9 and letters A-F, where A=10, B=11, C=12, D=13, E=14, F=15
One hex digit represents exactly 4 bits (a 'nibble'), so 2 hex digits represent one byte
Hex is commonly used for colors (#FF0000 = red), memory addresses, and error codes
To convert hex to binary, translate each hex digit into its 4-bit binary equivalent
Decimal (base-10) is what humans normally use; computers use binary internally for hardware simplicity

concepts.intro: Different kinds of data (numbers, text, images, sound) are all encoded into binary using agreed-upon schemes.
b: ASCII assigns each English letter, digit, and symbol a number from 0-127, stored as a byte
Unicode (like UTF-8) extends this to represent characters from virtually every language and emoji
Images are stored as grids of pixels, each pixel's color encoded as binary RGB values
Sound is captured by sampling the wave thousands of times per second and storing each sample as a number
File size depends on how much data is stored: more pixels, higher sample rates, or longer text mean larger files

concepts.intro: A computer's physical hardware works together, with each component playing a specialized role in processing information.
b: CPU: executes instructions; measured in GHz (clock speed) and number of cores
RAM: temporary, volatile working memory; more RAM lets more programs run smoothly at once
Storage (SSD/HDD): permanent, non-volatile; SSDs are faster than traditional spinning hard disks
Motherboard: connects all components together and lets them communicate
GPU: specialized processor originally for graphics, now also used for parallel computations like AI

concepts.intro: The operating system (OS) is software that manages hardware resources and provides a platform for other programs to run.
b: Examples of operating systems: Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS
The OS manages memory allocation, scheduling which program uses the CPU, and file storage
System software (like the OS) supports the computer itself; application software (like a browser) helps users do tasks
A file system organizes how data is stored and retrieved from storage devices
Drivers are small programs that let the OS communicate with specific hardware devices

keyFacts: 1 byte = 8 bits; 1 kilobyte (KB) ≈ 1000 bytes; 1 megabyte (MB) ≈ 1,000,000 bytes
Binary 1011 = decimal 11; decimal 25 = binary 11001
ASCII uses 7-8 bits per character; UTF-8 can use 1-4 bytes per character to support all languages
Moore's Law observed that transistor counts (and roughly computing power) doubled about every two years
traps: RAM is temporary/volatile working memory, not permanent storage — data in RAM is lost when power is off
A byte is 8 bits, not 10 bits — binary place values are powers of 2, not powers of 10
The CPU executes instructions; it is the GPU, not the CPU, that is optimized for massively parallel tasks like graphics
Hexadecimal is a human-friendly shorthand for binary, not a separate system computers use internally — hardware still stores everything in binary

units.name: Programming Fundamentals

concepts.intro: A variable is a named storage location that holds a value which can change while a program runs; every value has a data type that determines what operations are valid on it.
b: Common data types: integer (whole numbers), float/double (decimals), string (text), boolean (true/false)
A variable is created (declared) with a name and often an initial value, e.g., age = 16
Variable names should be descriptive and follow naming rules (no spaces, can't start with a digit)
Type matters: adding two integers gives a number, but adding two strings concatenates (joins) them
Some languages require declaring the type explicitly (statically typed); others infer it automatically (dynamically typed)

concepts.intro: Operators combine values and variables into expressions that produce a result, covering arithmetic, comparison, and logic.
b: Arithmetic operators: + (add), - (subtract), * (multiply), / (divide), % (modulo/remainder)
Comparison operators: == (equal), != (not equal), <, >, <=, >= — these produce a boolean result
Logical operators: AND, OR, NOT combine boolean expressions (e.g., age >= 13 AND age <= 19)
Order of operations (PEMDAS-like precedence) applies: multiplication/division before addition/subtraction
The assignment operator (=) stores a value into a variable; it is different from the equality operator (==)

concepts.intro: Programs typically follow a pattern of receiving input, processing it, and producing output, structured as a sequence of statements executed in order.
b: Output statements (like print) display information to the user
Input statements collect data from the user, often read in as a string that may need converting to a number
A statement is a single instruction; a program is a sequence of statements executed top to bottom by default
Comments (e.g., starting with # or //) are ignored by the computer but help humans understand code
Syntax errors occur when code doesn't follow a language's grammar rules and won't run at all

concepts.intro: Errors (bugs) are inevitable in programming; recognizing the type of error is the first step to fixing it.
b: Syntax errors: code violates the language's grammar rules (e.g., missing a colon or parenthesis)
Runtime errors: code is valid but fails while running (e.g., dividing by zero, opening a missing file)
Logic errors: code runs without crashing but produces the wrong result due to flawed reasoning
Debugging strategies include reading error messages carefully, using print statements to trace values, and testing small pieces separately
A debugger is a tool that lets you pause execution and inspect variable values step by step

concepts.intro: Good programming style makes code easier to read, test, and maintain, both for yourself and others.
b: Use meaningful variable and function names instead of single letters like x or temp
Keep consistent indentation to show code structure (especially important in Python)
Break repeated logic into functions rather than copy-pasting the same code multiple times
Test code with a range of inputs, including edge cases like zero, negative numbers, or empty strings
Version control (like Git) tracks changes to code over time and allows collaboration

concepts.intro: Programming languages provide different tools and styles for expressing solutions, but most fundamentals transfer between them.
b: Popular beginner languages include Python, JavaScript, and Java, each with different syntax but similar core concepts
A compiler translates entire source code into machine code before running; an interpreter executes code line by line
High-level languages (like Python) are closer to human language; low-level languages (like assembly) are closer to hardware
Procedural programming organizes code as a sequence of steps/functions; object-oriented programming organizes code around objects with data and behavior
Libraries and frameworks provide pre-written code so programmers don't have to solve common problems from scratch

keyFacts: The modulo operator (%) returns the remainder of division, e.g., 7 % 2 = 1
In most languages, = assigns a value while == checks for equality
Python uses indentation to define code blocks; languages like Java use curly braces {}
A compiler translates code before execution; an interpreter translates and runs it line-by-line
traps: = is assignment (stores a value), not ==, which is comparison (checks equality)
A syntax error prevents code from running at all; a logic error lets code run but produces a wrong answer, not a crash
Concatenating strings with + joins text together, not adds numbers — '2' + '2' gives '22' in many languages, not 4
Compiled and interpreted are about when/how code is translated, not about which language is 'better' — both approaches are valid

units.name: Control Flow & Functions

concepts.intro: Conditionals let a program make decisions, executing different code depending on whether a condition is true or false.
b: An if statement runs a block of code only when its condition evaluates to true
else runs when the if condition is false; else if (or elif) checks an additional condition
Conditions are boolean expressions, often built with comparison operators (==, <, >, etc.)
Nested conditionals place an if statement inside another to check multiple layers of logic
Only one branch of an if/elif/else chain executes per run, not multiple

concepts.intro: Loops let a program repeat a block of code multiple times without rewriting it, controlled by a counter or a condition.
b: A for loop typically repeats a fixed or known number of times, often iterating over a range or collection
A while loop repeats as long as a condition remains true, useful when the number of repetitions isn't known in advance
An infinite loop happens when the loop's condition never becomes false — a common bug to watch for
break exits a loop immediately; continue skips to the next iteration without finishing the current one
Loop variables (like i in 'for i in range(10)') track progress through the repetition

concepts.intro: A function is a reusable, named block of code that performs a task, optionally accepting inputs (parameters) and returning an output.
b: Defining a function specifies its name, parameters, and the code it runs when called
Calling a function executes its code, passing in specific values called arguments
A return statement sends a value back to wherever the function was called, ending the function
Parameters are placeholders in the function definition; arguments are the actual values passed in when calling
Functions with no explicit return statement typically return a special 'nothing' value (e.g., None in Python)

concepts.intro: Scope determines where in a program a variable can be accessed, which prevents naming conflicts and controls how data flows.
b: A local variable is defined inside a function and can only be used within that function
A global variable is defined outside all functions and can be accessed from anywhere in the program
Variables with the same name in different scopes are treated as entirely separate variables
Using too many global variables can make code harder to debug, since any function might change them
When a function ends, its local variables are typically destroyed and no longer accessible

concepts.intro: Real programs combine conditionals, loops, and functions together to build more complex, useful behavior.
b: A loop can contain a conditional inside it to make decisions on each iteration (e.g., check each item in a list)
A function can contain loops and conditionals inside its body to perform complex logic
Recursion is when a function calls itself to solve a smaller version of the same problem, eventually reaching a base case
Every recursive function needs a base case (a stopping condition) or it will run forever, similar to an infinite loop
Tracing through code step-by-step (mentally or on paper) helps verify control flow logic works as intended

concepts.intro: Certain patterns in control flow appear repeatedly across programs, along with common mistakes beginners make.
b: Accumulator pattern: use a variable (like total = 0) that updates inside a loop to build up a result
Off-by-one errors happen when a loop runs one time too many or too few, often from range/index miscounting
Forgetting to update a loop's counter or condition variable can cause an infinite loop
Comparing floats for exact equality can be unreliable due to how decimals are stored in binary
Testing loops and conditionals with boundary values (like 0, the first item, or the last item) catches many bugs

keyFacts: An if/elif/else chain executes exactly one branch per run, never more than one
A for loop is best when the number of repetitions is known; a while loop is best when it depends on a condition
Every function call with a return statement produces a value that can be stored or used elsewhere
A recursive function must have a base case to avoid infinite recursion
traps: break exits the loop entirely; continue skips only the current iteration and keeps looping — they are not the same
Parameters are the names in a function's definition; arguments are the actual values passed in when calling it
A local variable inside a function is not accessible outside it, even though a global variable with a similar name might exist
An infinite loop is a bug caused by a condition that never becomes false, not an intentional feature

units.name: Data Structures Intro

concepts.intro: An array (or list) stores multiple values together in a single ordered collection, each accessible by a numeric index.
b: Indexing typically starts at 0, so the first element is at index 0, the second at index 1, and so on
Arrays have a fixed size in many languages, while lists (like Python lists) can grow or shrink dynamically
Common operations include accessing an element by index, adding an element, removing an element, and searching
Accessing an element by index is fast (constant time), but searching for a value without knowing its index is slower
A 2D array (array of arrays) can represent grids, like a tic-tac-toe board or a spreadsheet

concepts.intro: Stacks and queues are ordered collections that restrict how you add and remove elements, following specific access patterns.
b: A stack follows LIFO (Last In, First Out): the most recently added item is the first one removed
Stack operations are called push (add to top) and pop (remove from top); think of a stack of plates
A queue follows FIFO (First In, First Out): the first item added is the first one removed
Queue operations are called enqueue (add to back) and dequeue (remove from front); think of a checkout line
Stacks are used for undo functionality and function call tracking; queues are used for task scheduling and print jobs

concepts.intro: A dictionary (also called a hash map or associative array) stores data as key-value pairs, letting you look up a value quickly using a unique key instead of a numeric index.
b: Each key in a dictionary must be unique; the value it maps to can be any data type, including another data structure
Looking up a value by its key is typically very fast (close to constant time) due to hashing
Common uses include storing a phone book (name to number), counting word frequency, or caching results
Unlike arrays, dictionaries are generally not ordered by position (though some modern languages preserve insertion order)
A hash function converts a key into an index internally, which is how fast lookups are achieved

concepts.intro: A set is a collection that stores only unique values, with no duplicates and typically no guaranteed order.
b: Adding a duplicate value to a set has no effect — the set still contains only one copy
Sets support operations like union (combine), intersection (common elements), and difference (elements in one but not another)
Checking whether a value exists in a set is typically very fast, similar to a dictionary lookup
Sets are useful for removing duplicates from a collection or quickly testing membership
Unlike a list, a set does not let you access elements by a numeric index

concepts.intro: Trees and graphs are structures used to represent hierarchical or interconnected data, going beyond simple linear sequences.
b: A tree consists of nodes connected by edges, starting from a root node, with each node having child nodes below it
A binary tree restricts each node to at most two children, often labeled left and right
A graph is a more general structure of nodes (vertices) connected by edges, which can represent networks like social connections or maps
Trees are used to represent file systems, organizational charts, and decision-making processes
Graphs can be 'directed' (edges have a one-way direction) or 'undirected' (edges go both ways)

concepts.intro: Different data structures have different strengths, and choosing the right one depends on what operations your program needs to perform efficiently.
b: Use an array/list when order matters and you need to access items by position
Use a stack when you need to process the most recently added item first (like undo history)
Use a queue when you need to process items in the order they arrived (like a task queue)
Use a dictionary when you need fast lookups by a meaningful key rather than a position
Use a set when you need to guarantee uniqueness or quickly check if something exists in a collection

keyFacts: Arrays/lists are zero-indexed in most programming languages: the first element is at index 0
Stack = LIFO (Last In, First Out); Queue = FIFO (First In, First Out)
Dictionary lookups by key are typically much faster than searching an unsorted list for a value
A set automatically eliminates duplicate values
traps: A stack is LIFO, not FIFO — the last item added is the first removed, unlike a queue
Accessing an array element by index is fast; searching for a value's position without an index is slower, especially in an unsorted array
Dictionaries are not guaranteed to be ordered by position the way arrays are (even if some languages preserve insertion order as an implementation detail)
A tree is a specific, hierarchical type of graph (no cycles, one root), not a completely separate unrelated concept from graphs

units.name: Algorithms & Problem Solving

concepts.intro: An algorithm is a precise, step-by-step procedure for solving a problem or completing a task, which a computer can follow exactly.
b: An algorithm must be unambiguous: each step must have exactly one clear meaning
An algorithm must eventually terminate (finish), unlike an infinite loop
The same problem can often be solved by multiple different algorithms, some more efficient than others
Pseudocode is an informal, human-readable way to describe an algorithm's steps before writing real code
A good algorithm should work correctly for all valid inputs, not just the examples it was designed for

concepts.intro: Searching algorithms find whether (and where) a target value exists within a collection of data.
b: Linear search checks each element one at a time from the start until it finds the target or reaches the end
Linear search works on unsorted data but can be slow for large collections since it may check every element
Binary search repeatedly cuts a sorted collection in half, comparing the middle element to the target
Binary search requires the data to be sorted first, but is much faster than linear search on large datasets
Binary search eliminates half the remaining possibilities with each comparison, making it very efficient

concepts.intro: Sorting algorithms arrange data into a specific order (like ascending numbers or alphabetical order), which is often a prerequisite for efficient searching.
b: Bubble sort repeatedly compares adjacent elements and swaps them if they're out of order, passing through the list multiple times
Selection sort repeatedly finds the smallest remaining element and moves it to its correct position
Bubble sort and selection sort are simple to understand but slow on large datasets compared to more advanced algorithms
Merge sort divides the data in half repeatedly, sorts each half, then merges the sorted halves back together (a 'divide and conquer' approach)
More advanced sorting algorithms (like merge sort or quicksort) scale much better to large amounts of data than simple sorts

concepts.intro: Big-O notation describes how an algorithm's running time (or memory use) grows as the size of its input grows, allowing comparison of efficiency independent of hardware.
b: O(1) — constant time: the operation takes the same amount of time regardless of input size (e.g., accessing an array element by index)
O(n) — linear time: time grows proportionally with input size (e.g., linear search checking every element once)
O(log n) — logarithmic time: time grows very slowly as input grows, by repeatedly cutting the problem in half (e.g., binary search)
O(n²) — quadratic time: time grows with the square of input size, often from nested loops over the same data (e.g., bubble sort)
Big-O focuses on the worst-case (or general) growth trend for large inputs, not exact timing on any one computer

concepts.intro: Effective problem solving in computer science often follows a repeatable process: understand, plan, implement, and test.
b: Break a large problem into smaller, more manageable subproblems (decomposition)
Look for patterns: has a similar problem been solved before, or can this be reduced to a known problem?
Abstraction means focusing on the important details of a problem while ignoring irrelevant complexity
Write pseudocode or draw a diagram/flowchart before jumping straight into code
Test your solution with simple cases first, then edge cases (like empty input or very large input)

concepts.intro: Choosing an algorithm often involves trade-offs between speed, memory usage, and simplicity, rather than one single 'best' choice.
b: A faster algorithm may use more memory (a common time-versus-space trade-off)
A simpler algorithm may be easier to write correctly but slower than a more complex, optimized one
For small inputs, a simple algorithm's inefficiency may not matter in practice
For large inputs, choosing an efficient algorithm (like binary search over linear search) can make a huge practical difference
Real-world engineering often favors 'good enough and correct' over 'theoretically fastest but error-prone'

keyFacts: Binary search requires sorted data and runs in O(log n) time, much faster than linear search's O(n) for large datasets
Bubble sort and selection sort run in O(n²) time, making them inefficient for large datasets
Big-O notation describes how runtime grows with input size, not the exact number of seconds a program takes
Decomposition (breaking a problem into smaller parts) is a foundational problem-solving strategy in computer science
traps: Binary search only works on sorted data — running it on unsorted data gives incorrect results
O(log n) is much faster than O(n) for large inputs, not slower — logarithmic growth is very slow-growing, which is good
Big-O describes growth trends for large inputs, not a literal count of seconds or a guarantee about small inputs
An algorithm that works on the example given isn't automatically correct — it must be verified against edge cases and all valid inputs

units.name: Web & Internet How It Works

concepts.intro: The internet is a global network of interconnected computers, while the World Wide Web is a system of linked documents (websites) that runs on top of that network.
b: The internet is the physical/logical infrastructure: cables, routers, satellites, and protocols connecting devices worldwide
The Web (WWW) is one application that uses the internet, alongside others like email and file transfer
A network is any group of connected devices that can share data; the internet is a 'network of networks'
Data on the internet travels in small chunks called packets, which are reassembled at the destination
The internet has no single owner; it operates through cooperating networks following shared standard protocols

concepts.intro: Every device on the internet needs a unique address to send and receive data, and a naming system to make those addresses human-friendly.
b: An IP address (like 192.168.1.1) is a numeric label uniquely identifying a device on a network
IPv4 addresses use four numbers (0-255) separated by dots; IPv6 was created because IPv4 addresses were running out
DNS (Domain Name System) translates human-readable domain names (like google.com) into numeric IP addresses
Without DNS, users would need to memorize IP addresses instead of easy-to-remember website names
A domain name is registered and can point to different IP addresses over time as servers change

concepts.intro: Loading a website involves a client (your browser) requesting data from a server, which responds with the content to display.
b: A client is the device/program requesting a resource (typically a web browser); a server stores and provides resources
HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) is the set of rules browsers and servers use to communicate requests and responses
HTTPS is the secure version of HTTP, encrypting data in transit using SSL/TLS so it can't easily be intercepted
A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) specifies the address of a resource, including protocol, domain, and path
HTML structures a webpage's content, CSS styles its appearance, and JavaScript adds interactivity

concepts.l: HTTP Requests, Responses, and Status Codes
concepts.intro: Communication between a browser and server follows a request-response pattern, with standardized codes indicating the outcome.
b: Common HTTP methods: GET (retrieve data), POST (send/submit data), PUT (update data), DELETE (remove data)
A 200 status code means 'OK' — the request succeeded
A 404 status code means 'Not Found' — the requested resource doesn't exist at that address
A 500 status code means 'Internal Server Error' — something went wrong on the server's side
Cookies are small pieces of data a server asks a browser to store, often used for login sessions or preferences

concepts.intro: Building websites typically combines structural, visual, and behavioral layers, alongside a place to store and serve the site.
b: HTML (HyperText Markup Language) uses tags to define the structure and content of a webpage, like headings and paragraphs
CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) controls a webpage's visual presentation: colors, fonts, layout, spacing
JavaScript is a programming language that runs in the browser to make web pages interactive and dynamic
Front-end development focuses on what users see and interact with directly (client-side)
Back-end development focuses on servers, databases, and logic that runs behind the scenes (server-side)

concepts.intro: Understanding how networks are structured and protected is foundational to using the internet safely.
b: A firewall monitors and controls incoming/outgoing network traffic based on security rules
Encryption scrambles data so only someone with the correct key can read it, protecting data in transit or storage
A Wi-Fi router connects devices within a local network and typically connects that network to the wider internet
Bandwidth measures how much data can be transferred over a network connection in a given time
Public Wi-Fi networks are riskier than private ones because data may be more easily intercepted by others on the same network

keyFacts: DNS translates human-readable domain names into numeric IP addresses
HTTPS encrypts data between browser and server; HTTP does not
A 404 status code means the requested resource was not found; a 200 means success
HTML structures content, CSS styles it, and JavaScript adds interactivity
traps: The internet and the World Wide Web are not the same thing — the Web is a service (linked documents) that runs on top of the internet infrastructure
HTTPS is not just 'HTTP but newer' — it specifically adds encryption (via SSL/TLS) to protect data in transit
A 404 error means the resource wasn't found, not that the whole internet is down — it's specific to that URL/request
IP addresses identify devices numerically; domain names are the human-friendly labels DNS maps to those numbers, not the reverse

units.name: Data & Privacy

concepts.intro: Encryption scrambles readable data (plaintext) into unreadable data (ciphertext) using a key, so only someone with the right key can reverse the process.
b: Symmetric encryption uses the same key to encrypt and decrypt (fast, but the key must be shared secretly, e.g. AES)
Asymmetric encryption uses a public key to encrypt and a private key to decrypt — the public key can be shared openly (e.g. RSA)
HTTPS uses a combination: asymmetric encryption to safely exchange a symmetric session key, then symmetric encryption for the actual data
Hashing is different from encryption: a hash is one-way and cannot be reversed, used to verify passwords or file integrity without storing the original
The lock icon in a browser means the connection is encrypted (HTTPS/TLS), not that the website itself is trustworthy
Longer keys and modern algorithms resist brute-force attacks; outdated algorithms (like old DES) can be cracked with enough computing power

concepts.intro: A data breach happens when unauthorized parties gain access to sensitive stored data, often through stolen credentials, software vulnerabilities, or social engineering.
b: Common causes include weak/reused passwords, unpatched software, phishing attacks, and misconfigured databases left publicly accessible
Breached data often includes usernames, passwords, credit card numbers, or personal identifiers, which attackers sell or use for identity theft
Companies mitigate damage by hashing and salting stored passwords, so a stolen database doesn't reveal plaintext passwords
Two-factor authentication (2FA) limits damage from breaches: even a stolen password isn't enough to log in without the second factor
After a breach, best practice is to notify affected users, force password resets, and patch the vulnerability that caused it
Reusing the same password across sites means one breach can compromise all your other accounts (credential stuffing)

concepts.intro: Cookies are small pieces of data websites store in your browser to remember information between visits, such as login state, preferences, or browsing behavior.
b: First-party cookies are set by the site you're visiting (e.g. keeping you logged in); third-party cookies are set by other domains embedded on the page (e.g. ad networks)
Third-party cookies enable cross-site tracking: an advertiser can see that the same browser visited many different sites, building a behavior profile
Session cookies expire when you close the browser; persistent cookies remain until their expiration date or you delete them
Browsers increasingly block third-party cookies by default, pushing advertisers toward alternatives like device fingerprinting
Local storage and web storage are similar to cookies but hold more data and aren't automatically sent with every request
Clearing cookies logs you out of sites and removes tracking history, but doesn't remove data already collected by trackers

concepts.intro: Privacy laws like the EU's GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation) give individuals rights over their personal data and require organizations to handle it responsibly.
b: Core rights include the right to access your data, the right to correct it, and the right to erasure ("right to be forgotten")
Companies must obtain clear, informed consent before collecting personal data — pre-checked boxes or buried fine print don't count
Data minimization means collecting only the data actually needed for a stated purpose, not everything possible
Organizations must report data breaches to regulators and affected users within a set time frame (72 hours under GDPR)
GDPR applies to any company handling EU residents' data, regardless of where the company is based, which is why many global sites show cookie consent banners
Violations can result in significant fines, calculated as a percentage of a company's global revenue

concepts.intro: Cybersecurity is the practice of protecting systems, networks, and data from unauthorized access, damage, or disruption.
b: Phishing tricks users into revealing credentials or installing malware by impersonating a trusted source (email, text, or fake website)
Malware is a broad term for malicious software: viruses attach to files and spread, worms self-replicate across networks, and ransomware encrypts files and demands payment
A firewall filters network traffic based on rules, blocking unauthorized access while allowing legitimate traffic through
The principle of least privilege means giving users and programs only the access they need to do their job, limiting damage if an account is compromised
Software updates and patches fix known security vulnerabilities — delaying updates leaves systems exposed to attacks that already have public exploits
Social engineering exploits human trust rather than technical flaws, making user awareness a critical defense alongside technical safeguards

keyFacts: Encryption scrambles data reversibly with a key; hashing transforms data one-way and cannot be reversed.
HTTPS combines asymmetric encryption (to exchange a key) with symmetric encryption (to protect the actual data).
GDPR gives users rights to access, correct, and erase their personal data, and requires breach notification within 72 hours.
Two-factor authentication and unique passwords are the most effective everyday defenses against account breaches.
traps: A hash is one-way and cannot be decrypted, not a form of encryption you can reverse with a key.
The HTTPS padlock means the connection is encrypted, not that the site itself is safe or legitimate.
Third-party cookies enable cross-site tracking; first-party cookies just support the site you're actually visiting, not ad networks.
Clearing your cookies removes local tracking data, not the data companies already collected and stored on their servers.

units.name: Ethics & Careers

concepts.intro: Algorithmic bias occurs when a computer system produces systematically unfair outcomes for certain groups, usually because of biased training data or flawed design choices, not because a program is intentionally programmed to discriminate.
b: Bias often comes from training data that reflects historical human bias — a hiring algorithm trained on past resumes may learn to favor the same demographics that were historically hired
Underrepresentation in training data (e.g. facial recognition trained mostly on lighter-skinned faces) can make a system perform worse for underrepresented groups
Proxy variables can encode bias indirectly: a model might not use race directly but use zip code, which correlates strongly with race in many places
Feedback loops can worsen bias over time: a biased predictive policing model sends more patrols to a neighborhood, generates more arrests there, and 'confirms' its own bias
Auditing models for disparate impact across groups (not just overall accuracy) is a key technique for catching bias before deployment
Removing a sensitive attribute (like race) from a dataset does not guarantee fairness, since other correlated features can still encode it

concepts.intro: AI ethics addresses the responsibilities that come with building and deploying artificial intelligence systems that can affect people's lives, rights, and opportunities.
b: Transparency means users and affected people can understand, at some level, how and why an AI system reached a decision
Accountability means a person or organization — not 'the algorithm' — is responsible when an AI system causes harm
Explainability is especially important in high-stakes domains like healthcare, lending, or criminal justice, where a wrong or opaque decision has serious consequences
Privacy concerns arise because many AI systems are trained on large amounts of personal data, sometimes collected without full user awareness or consent
The trolley-problem style dilemmas around autonomous vehicles illustrate that AI systems can face genuine ethical trade-offs, not just technical bugs
Deepfakes and generative AI raise new ethical questions around consent, misinformation, and the erosion of trust in audio/video evidence

concepts.intro: Intellectual property (IP) law protects creative and technical work; in software, licenses define exactly how others are legally allowed to use, modify, and distribute that work.
b: Copyright automatically protects original code and creative work the moment it's created, giving the creator exclusive rights to copy, modify, and distribute it
Open-source licenses (like MIT or GPL) grant others permission to use and modify code, but under specific conditions the license spells out
Permissive licenses (MIT, Apache) allow nearly unrestricted reuse, even in proprietary closed-source products, as long as attribution is kept
Copyleft licenses (like GPL) require that any derivative work using the code must also be released under the same open license — this is sometimes called a 'viral' license
Patents protect novel inventions or processes (including some software methods) for a limited time, preventing others from using them without a license
Using someone else's code without checking its license, or violating a license's terms (e.g. shipping GPL code in closed-source software), can create real legal liability

concepts.intro: The tech industry offers many distinct career paths that require different skill combinations, from writing code to designing systems to analyzing data.
b: Software engineers design, build, and maintain applications and systems; roles often specialize into front-end (user interfaces), back-end (servers/databases), or full-stack (both)
Data scientists and data analysts extract insights from data, often using statistics, programming (like Python or SQL), and visualization tools
UX/UI designers focus on how usable and intuitive a product feels, blending research, psychology, and visual design rather than writing production code
DevOps and systems/network engineers keep infrastructure running reliably — deploying code, managing servers, and ensuring uptime and security
Cybersecurity specialists focus on protecting systems from attacks, including roles like penetration testers who are hired to find vulnerabilities before attackers do
A traditional four-year degree is one path into tech, but bootcamps, certifications, self-teaching, and portfolios of personal projects are all recognized alternative routes

concepts.intro: Questions on this unit test whether you can identify real ethical failure modes and distinguish them from unrelated technical concepts covered elsewhere in the course.
b: Expect scenario-based questions: you'll be given a situation (a biased hiring tool, a scraped dataset, a mislabeled license) and asked to name the underlying issue
Distinguish between bias in data, bias in algorithm design, and bias in how a system's output is used by humans — exam questions often hinge on this distinction
Know the difference between copyright, patents, and licenses — they're related but protect different things and are tested separately
Be ready to distinguish an ethical/legal question (should we do this?) from a purely technical one (can we do this?) — both types appear, but they test different reasoning
Career-path questions test whether you know which role does which kind of work, not just that the roles exist

keyFacts: Algorithmic bias usually comes from biased or unrepresentative training data, not from an explicit intent to discriminate.
Removing a sensitive attribute from a dataset does not eliminate bias if correlated proxy variables (like zip code) remain.
Copyleft licenses (like GPL) require derivative works to be released under the same license; permissive licenses (like MIT) do not.
Accountability in AI ethics means a person or organization is responsible for an AI system's harms — not the algorithm itself.
traps: Algorithmic bias is usually the result of skewed training data or flawed design, not deliberate programmer intent to discriminate.
A permissive license like MIT allows use in closed-source software; a copyleft license like GPL requires derivatives to stay open-source — mixing them up is a common exam trap.
Copyright protects creative/expressive works automatically at creation, while a patent must be formally applied for and approved to protect an invention or process.
High overall accuracy does not prove a model is fair — it can still perform far worse for specific subgroups, which is why disparate-impact audits matter.

quiz.q: What is the base of the binary number system?
quiz.e: Binary is base-2, using only digits 0 and 1.

quiz.q: How many bits are in one byte?
quiz.e: A byte is defined as a group of 8 bits.

quiz.q: What is the decimal value of binary 1011?
What is the decimal value of binary 1000?
quiz.e: 1000 has a 1 in the 8's place, so it equals 8.

quiz.q: Which component is volatile, meaning it loses its contents when power is off?
quiz.e: RAM is volatile memory used for temporary working data.

quiz.q: What does CPU stand for?
quiz.e: CPU stands for Central Processing Unit, the 'brain' of the computer.

quiz.q: What number system uses digits 0-9 and letters A-F?
quiz.e: Hexadecimal (base-16) uses 0-9 and A-F to represent values 0-15.

quiz.q: How many bits does one hexadecimal digit represent?
quiz.e: Each hex digit maps to exactly 4 bits (a nibble).

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of an operating system?
o: To manage hardware resources and run other software
quiz.e: The OS manages memory, CPU scheduling, and hardware so other programs can run.

quiz.q: Which encoding standard supports characters from nearly every language, including emoji?
quiz.e: Unicode (commonly encoded as UTF-8) extends ASCII to support global characters.

quiz.q: What does the fetch-decode-execute cycle describe?
o: How data is saved to disk
quiz.e: This cycle describes the basic steps a CPU repeats to run a program.

quiz.q: Which of these is non-volatile storage?
quiz.e: SSDs retain data even without power, unlike RAM.

quiz.q: Convert decimal 6 to binary.
quiz.e: 6 = 4+2, so binary is 110.

quiz.q: Convert decimal 13 to binary.
quiz.e: 13 = 8+4+1, so binary is 1101.

quiz.q: What is a bit?
quiz.e: A bit is the smallest unit of data, either 0 or 1.

quiz.q: Approximately how many bytes are in a megabyte?
quiz.e: A megabyte is approximately one million bytes.

quiz.q: Which device would be classified as an input device?
quiz.e: A keyboard sends data into the computer, making it an input device.

quiz.q: What is the role of a GPU?
o: Handling parallel computations, especially graphics and AI
quiz.e: GPUs are optimized for parallel processing tasks like rendering graphics.

quiz.q: Why do computers use binary instead of decimal internally?
o: Binary is easier for humans to read
Transistors are simplest to build as two-state (on/off) switches
Binary uses less power than decimal
quiz.e: Two-state electrical switches map naturally onto binary's two digits.

quiz.q: What is the hexadecimal representation of decimal 255?
quiz.e: 255 in binary is 11111111, which splits into two nibbles of 1111 (F) each: FF.

quiz.q: What does ASCII primarily encode?
quiz.e: ASCII assigns numeric codes to letters, digits, and symbols.

quiz.q: What is clock speed typically measured in?
quiz.e: Clock speed, measuring CPU cycles per second, is measured in Hertz (e.g., GHz).

quiz.q: Which best distinguishes system software from application software?
o: System software supports the computer itself; application software helps users do tasks
quiz.e: The OS is system software; a browser or game is application software.

quiz.q: What happens to data stored only in RAM when the computer loses power?
o: It is automatically saved to the cloud
quiz.e: RAM is volatile, so unsaved data in RAM disappears when power is cut.

quiz.q: What is a 'driver' in the context of an operating system?
o: A person who codes the OS
A program that lets the OS communicate with specific hardware
quiz.e: Drivers translate between the OS and hardware devices like printers or graphics cards.

quiz.q: Which is an example of an operating system?
quiz.e: Linux is an operating system; the others are application software.

quiz.q: How is color often represented in web design?
quiz.e: Web colors are commonly written as 6-digit hex codes representing red, green, and blue values.

quiz.q: What does it mean for storage to be 'non-volatile'?
o: It retains data even when power is removed
quiz.e: Non-volatile storage like an SSD keeps data without continuous power.

quiz.q: What is a nibble?
quiz.e: A nibble is half a byte, or 4 bits, matching one hex digit.

quiz.q: Which best describes 'Moore's Law'?
o: An observation that transistor density roughly doubles every two years
quiz.e: Moore's Law is an observed trend in transistor miniaturization and growth, not a physical law.

quiz.q: What number system do humans typically use in daily life?
quiz.e: Humans generally count using base-10 (decimal), likely due to having ten fingers.

quiz.q: Which best describes how images are digitally stored?
o: As a grid of pixels, each with color values
quiz.e: Digital images are grids of pixels, each pixel storing color as binary data (e.g., RGB values).

quiz.q: What is the motherboard's function?
o: Physically connects and enables communication between components
quiz.e: The motherboard is the main circuit board linking CPU, RAM, storage, and other parts.

What best explains why SSDs are generally preferred over traditional hard drives (HDDs)?
o: SSDs have no moving parts and are faster
quiz.e: SSDs use flash memory with no moving parts, making them faster and more durable than spinning HDDs.

quiz.q: What is the largest value a single byte (8 bits) can represent in unsigned binary?
quiz.e: 8 bits can represent 2^8 = 256 values, from 0 to 255.

quiz.q: Which pair correctly matches a unit with what it measures?
quiz.e: Hertz measures frequency/clock speed; bytes measure storage size.

quiz.q: What is sampling, in the context of digital audio?
o: Measuring a sound wave's amplitude at regular intervals to store as numbers
quiz.e: Digital audio is created by sampling the analog wave repeatedly and storing each measurement as a binary number.

quiz.q: Why might a text file be smaller than an image file of similar content length?
o: Text always compresses better than images by law
Images generally require far more data per unit of content (many pixels vs. characters)
Image files use binary, but text files do not
quiz.e: Images typically require storing information for many pixels, resulting in much larger raw data compared to compact character-based text.

quiz.q: What best describes the relationship between hardware and software?
o: Hardware is the physical machine; software is the instructions that tell hardware what to do
Software replaces the need for hardware
Hardware only exists in the cloud
quiz.e: Hardware is physical components; software consists of programs/instructions that control hardware behavior.

quiz.q: What is a variable in programming?
o: A fixed value that never changes
A named storage location that holds a value which can change
quiz.e: Variables store data that can be updated as the program runs.

quiz.q: Which data type would best store the value 3.14?
quiz.e: 3.14 has a decimal point, so it is a float (floating-point number).

quiz.q: What does the modulo operator (%) return?
quiz.e: Modulo returns the remainder of dividing one number by another.

quiz.q: What is the result of 7 % 2?
quiz.e: 7 divided by 2 is 3 remainder 1, so 7 % 2 = 1.

quiz.q: What does the == operator do?
o: Assigns a value to a variable
Checks if two values are equal
quiz.e: == is the equality comparison operator, returning true or false.

quiz.q: What kind of error occurs when code violates the grammar rules of a language?
quiz.e: Syntax errors happen when code doesn't follow the language's required structure.

quiz.q: What kind of error lets a program run but produces an incorrect result?
quiz.e: A logic error means the code runs, but the reasoning/algorithm is flawed.

quiz.q: What kind of error happens while a program is running, such as dividing by zero?
quiz.e: Runtime errors occur during execution, even if the syntax is valid.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a comment in code?
o: To be executed as an instruction
To explain code to human readers; it is ignored by the computer
quiz.e: Comments are notes for humans and are not executed by the program.

quiz.q: Which best describes a compiler?
o: A tool that translates the entire program into machine code before it runs
A tool that only checks spelling
A tool that deletes bugs automatically
quiz.e: Compilers translate the whole source code into machine code ahead of execution.

quiz.q: Which best describes an interpreter?
o: It compiles code once and never again
It executes code line-by-line, translating as it goes
It only works with binary files
quiz.e: Interpreters read and execute code one line/statement at a time.

quiz.q: In most languages, what is the difference between = and ==?
o: = assigns a value; == compares for equality
== assigns a value; = compares for equality
quiz.e: = stores a value into a variable, while == checks whether two values are equal.

quiz.q: What will '2' + '2' likely produce in many programming languages, where both values are strings?
quiz.e: Adding two strings typically concatenates them rather than performing math.

quiz.q: Which is an example of a boolean value?
quiz.e: Boolean values are only True or False.

quiz.q: What does an input statement typically do?
quiz.e: Input statements gather data (often as text) from the user during execution.

quiz.q: Why might input read from a user need to be converted before doing math with it?
o: Input is always already a number
Input is often read as a string/text, even if it looks like a number
Math cannot be performed in programs
quiz.e: Many languages read user input as text (a string), which must be converted to a numeric type for arithmetic.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of using functions instead of repeating code?
o: To avoid duplicating logic and make code reusable/organized
To increase the number of syntax errors
quiz.e: Functions let you reuse the same logic without copy-pasting it repeatedly.

quiz.q: What does 'static typing' mean?
o: Variable types are declared and fixed, checked before running
quiz.e: Statically typed languages require explicit types that are checked before the program runs.

quiz.q: What does 'dynamic typing' mean, as used in Python?
o: Variable types are determined automatically at runtime and can change
The language has no data types
quiz.e: Dynamically typed languages infer types automatically, and a variable's type can change.

quiz.q: What is version control (e.g., Git) primarily used for?
o: Tracking changes to code over time and enabling collaboration
quiz.e: Version control tracks historical changes and helps multiple people collaborate on code.

quiz.q: What does a debugger allow a programmer to do?
o: Pause execution and inspect variable values step by step
quiz.e: A debugger lets you step through code and examine program state to find bugs.

quiz.q: Which is considered a 'high-level' programming language?
quiz.e: Python is high-level, meaning its syntax is closer to human language than to hardware instructions.

quiz.q: What is an 'edge case' in testing?
o: An unusual or extreme input, like zero or an empty string, that might break code
quiz.e: Edge cases test boundary or unusual conditions that often reveal bugs.

quiz.q: What does the order of operations (operator precedence) determine?
o: The order in which parts of an expression are evaluated
quiz.e: Precedence rules dictate, e.g., that multiplication happens before addition unless parentheses override it.

quiz.q: Which logical operator returns true only if both conditions are true?
quiz.e: AND requires both operands to be true for the result to be true.

quiz.q: What does the NOT operator do to a boolean value?
o: Flips true to false and false to true
quiz.e: NOT inverts a boolean's value.

quiz.q: What is object-oriented programming primarily organized around?
o: A strict sequence of unrelated steps
Objects that bundle data and behavior together
quiz.e: OOP structures code as objects that combine data (attributes) and behavior (methods).

quiz.q: What is procedural programming primarily organized around?
o: Sequences of steps/functions performed in order
quiz.e: Procedural programming follows a step-by-step, function-based approach to solving problems.

quiz.q: Why use meaningful variable names like 'totalScore' instead of 'x'?
o: It makes the program run faster
It makes code more readable and easier to maintain
It is required by all compilers
quiz.e: Descriptive names improve readability without affecting program speed or correctness.

quiz.q: What is a library or framework in programming?
o: A physical building for storing computers
Pre-written code that provides reusable functionality
quiz.e: Libraries and frameworks give programmers reusable, pre-built code for common tasks.

quiz.q: What best describes 'concatenation' with strings?
o: Joining two or more strings together
quiz.e: Concatenation combines strings end-to-end, often using the + operator.

quiz.q: Which best explains why indentation matters in Python specifically?
o: It is purely stylistic and has no effect on the program
Python uses indentation to define code blocks/structure
quiz.e: Unlike many languages that use braces, Python relies on indentation to define blocks of code.

quiz.q: What happens if you try to divide a number by zero at runtime in many languages?
o: It typically causes a runtime error/exception
quiz.e: Division by zero is undefined and commonly raises a runtime error.

quiz.q: What is the result of the expression 2 + 3 * 4, following standard operator precedence?
quiz.e: Multiplication happens first (3*4=12), then addition: 2+12=14.

quiz.q: Which statement about testing with a range of inputs is most accurate?
o: Testing should include typical, boundary, and invalid inputs to catch bugs
Testing is unnecessary if code compiles
Only professional programmers need to test code
quiz.e: Thorough testing covers typical cases plus edge cases and invalid inputs.

quiz.q: What is a 'string' data type used for?
quiz.e: A string stores sequences of characters, i.e., text.

quiz.q: Why might a program with correct syntax still give the wrong answer?
o: This is impossible if syntax is correct
It may contain a logic error in its reasoning or algorithm
quiz.e: Syntax correctness only means the code will run — it doesn't guarantee the logic behind it is right.

quiz.q: What does 'readable code' primarily help with?
o: Helping humans understand, maintain, and debug the code later
Avoiding the need for an operating system
quiz.e: Readable code is easier for the original author or others to understand and maintain over time.

quiz.q: Which is an example of an arithmetic operator?
quiz.e: * (multiplication) is an arithmetic operator; the others are logical/comparison operators.

quiz.q: What does it mean for a program to execute 'top to bottom' by default?
o: Statements run in the order they are written unless control flow changes that
The last line always runs first
Only the first line ever executes
quiz.e: Without loops, conditionals, or function calls redirecting flow, a program executes statements sequentially from top to bottom.

quiz.q: What does an if statement do?
o: Repeats code a fixed number of times
Runs a block of code only if a condition is true
quiz.e: An if statement conditionally executes code based on a boolean condition.

quiz.q: When does the else block execute?
o: Always, regardless of the if condition
Only when the preceding if (and any elif) conditions are false
Before the if condition is checked
quiz.e: else runs when none of the preceding conditions in the chain were true.

quiz.q: What type of loop is best when you know exactly how many times to repeat?
quiz.e: For loops are typically used for a known/fixed number of iterations.

quiz.q: What type of loop is best when repetition depends on a condition that may vary?
quiz.e: While loops repeat as long as a condition remains true, which suits variable-length repetition.

quiz.q: What does the break statement do inside a loop?
quiz.e: break immediately terminates the loop it's inside.

quiz.q: What does the continue statement do inside a loop?
o: Skips the rest of the current iteration and proceeds to the next one
quiz.e: continue skips remaining code in the current iteration but keeps the loop running.

quiz.q: What is an infinite loop?
o: A loop that runs exactly once
A loop whose condition never becomes false, so it never stops
A function with no return value
quiz.e: Infinite loops occur when the stopping condition is never met.

quiz.q: What is a function in programming?
o: A reusable, named block of code that performs a task
quiz.e: Functions are reusable blocks of code that can be called by name.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a parameter and an argument?
o: They are exactly the same thing
A parameter is the placeholder in a function's definition; an argument is the actual value passed in
An argument is defined in the function; a parameter is passed at call time
quiz.e: Parameters are named in the function definition; arguments are the real values supplied when calling.

quiz.q: What does a return statement do?
o: Sends a value back to the caller and ends the function
quiz.e: return sends a result back to wherever the function was called and exits the function.

quiz.q: What is a local variable?
o: A variable accessible from anywhere in the program
A variable defined inside a function, accessible only within that function
quiz.e: Local variables exist only within the function (or block) where they are defined.

quiz.q: What is a global variable?
o: A variable defined outside all functions, accessible throughout the program
A variable only usable inside one function
A constant that cannot be read
quiz.e: Global variables are declared outside functions and can be accessed from many parts of a program.

quiz.q: What is recursion?
o: A function calling itself to solve a smaller version of the same problem
quiz.e: Recursion involves a function invoking itself, typically breaking a problem into smaller subproblems.

quiz.q: What must every correctly written recursive function have?
o: A base case that stops the recursion
quiz.e: A base case prevents infinite recursion by giving a stopping condition.

quiz.q: What is an off-by-one error?
o: A bug where a loop runs one time too many or too few
An error only in recursive functions
quiz.e: Off-by-one errors often stem from miscounting loop bounds or indices.

quiz.q: In a chain of if/elif/else, how many branches execute per run?
quiz.e: Only the first branch whose condition is true (or the else, if none match) executes.

quiz.q: What happens to a function's local variables after the function finishes running?
o: They are typically destroyed and no longer accessible
They are saved to disk automatically
quiz.e: Local variables generally disappear once their function call ends.

quiz.q: What is the 'accumulator pattern' commonly used for?
o: Building up a result (like a sum or count) using a variable updated inside a loop
quiz.e: An accumulator variable (e.g., total = 0) updates each loop iteration to build a cumulative result.

quiz.q: Why can comparing floating-point numbers for exact equality be unreliable?
o: Floats cannot be compared at all
Decimal values may not be stored with perfect precision in binary
This is never actually a problem
quiz.e: Due to binary representation limits, floats can have tiny rounding errors that break exact equality checks.

quiz.q: What does nesting a conditional inside another conditional allow?
quiz.e: Nested if statements let a program evaluate additional conditions within an already-true branch.

quiz.q: If a function has no explicit return statement, what does it typically return (e.g., in Python)?
quiz.e: Without an explicit return, many languages return a null/None-like value by default.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of an accidental infinite loop?
o: Using a for loop instead of while
Forgetting to update the loop's condition variable so it never becomes false
quiz.e: If nothing changes the value being tested, a while loop's condition may never become false.

quiz.q: Which best describes tracing through code?
o: Manually stepping through code line by line to verify its logic
Only running code with a debugger tool
quiz.e: Tracing involves mentally or manually following execution to understand or verify program behavior.

quiz.q: What kind of expression does an if statement's condition need to evaluate to?
quiz.e: Conditions must resolve to a boolean value to decide which branch runs.

quiz.q: Why is testing boundary values (like the first or last item) important?
o: Boundary/edge cases often reveal bugs that typical inputs don't
It only matters for recursive functions
quiz.e: Edge cases frequently expose issues like off-by-one errors that mid-range inputs wouldn't.

quiz.q: What best distinguishes a function definition from a function call?
o: Definition creates the function's code; a call executes it with specific arguments
A call happens before a definition always
quiz.e: You define a function once, then call (invoke) it as many times as needed with arguments.

quiz.q: Which is a valid reason to use a while loop instead of a for loop?
o: The number of iterations is unknown and depends on a condition, like waiting for valid input
You want to repeat exactly 10 times
You need to define a function
You want to avoid using variables
quiz.e: While loops suit situations where the stopping point depends on a runtime condition, not a fixed count.

quiz.q: What happens if a recursive function is missing a base case?
o: It runs once and stops safely
It will recurse infinitely (or until a stack/memory error occurs)
quiz.e: Without a base case, recursive calls never stop, eventually causing a stack overflow or crash.

quiz.q: What is scope, in programming?
o: The region of code where a variable can be accessed
quiz.e: Scope defines where in the code a variable's name is valid and accessible.

quiz.q: Why might overusing global variables make debugging harder?
o: Global variables don't actually exist in most languages
Any function could modify a global variable, making it hard to track where a bug originated
Global variables always cause syntax errors
They make programs run faster with fewer bugs
quiz.e: Because many parts of a program can alter a global variable, tracing unexpected changes becomes difficult.

quiz.q: In 'for i in range(5):', how many times will the loop body typically execute?
quiz.e: range(5) produces 5 values (0 through 4), so the loop runs 5 times.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of combining loops and conditionals together?
o: It is not possible in most languages
To make decisions on each iteration of a repeated process, like checking each item in a list
To eliminate the need for functions
quiz.e: Nesting a conditional inside a loop lets a program evaluate each item or step individually.

quiz.q: Which best describes why functions improve code organization?
o: They make code longer and harder to read
They let you name and reuse logic instead of duplicating it everywhere
They are required by every programming language
They eliminate the need for variables
quiz.e: Functions package logic into reusable, named units, reducing duplication and improving clarity.

quiz.q: What does it mean when a variable defined inside a function 'shadows' a global variable of the same name?
o: The global variable is permanently deleted
Inside the function, the local variable takes precedence over the global one with the same name
quiz.e: A local variable with the same name as a global one takes priority within its own scope, without deleting the global.

quiz.q: Which loop structure would best handle 'keep asking the user for input until they enter a valid number'?
o: A for loop with a fixed range
A while loop tied to a validity condition
quiz.e: Since the number of attempts is unknown in advance, a while loop tied to input validity fits best.

quiz.q: What is the term for calling a function from inside its own definition?
quiz.e: A function calling itself is recursion.

quiz.q: Which statement about function calls is correct?
o: A function can only be called once in a program
A function can be called multiple times with different arguments
Arguments must always match parameter names exactly
Functions cannot accept more than one parameter
quiz.e: Functions are reusable and can be invoked repeatedly with different argument values.

quiz.q: What does it mean if a while loop's condition is checked before each iteration, including the first?
o: The loop body might execute zero times if the condition starts false
The loop body always executes at least once
The loop is guaranteed to be infinite
quiz.e: A standard while loop tests its condition before running the body, so it may never execute if false initially.

quiz.q: Which best describes why breaking a large problem into functions helps with debugging?
o: Each function can be tested and reasoned about independently
It removes the need for return statements
quiz.e: Smaller, isolated functions are easier to test and pinpoint bugs in.

quiz.q: What is the effect of placing a return statement in the middle of a function?
o: It immediately exits the function, skipping any remaining code below it
It pauses the function until called again
quiz.e: A return statement ends function execution immediately, wherever it appears.

quiz.q: In most programming languages, what index does the first element of an array have?
quiz.e: Most languages use zero-based indexing, so the first element is index 0.

quiz.q: What does LIFO stand for, describing a stack?
quiz.e: LIFO means the last item added is the first one removed, like a stack of plates.

quiz.q: What does FIFO stand for, describing a queue?
quiz.e: FIFO means the first item added is the first one removed, like a checkout line.

quiz.q: What is the term for adding an item to the top of a stack?
quiz.e: Push adds an item to the top of a stack.

quiz.q: What is the term for removing an item from the top of a stack?
quiz.e: Pop removes and returns the top item of a stack.

quiz.q: What is the term for adding an item to the back of a queue?
quiz.e: Enqueue adds an item to the back (end) of a queue.

quiz.q: What is the term for removing an item from the front of a queue?
quiz.e: Dequeue removes the item from the front of a queue.

quiz.q: What is a dictionary (hash map) primarily used for?
o: Storing items only by numeric position
Storing key-value pairs for fast lookup by key
quiz.e: Dictionaries map unique keys to values for fast retrieval.

quiz.q: What must be true about keys in a dictionary?
quiz.e: Each key in a dictionary must be unique, though values can repeat.

o: A set can contain duplicates; a list cannot
A set stores only unique values; a list can contain duplicates
Sets are always sorted; lists are not

quiz.q: Which operation checks if two sets share any common elements?
quiz.e: Intersection returns the elements common to both sets.

quiz.q: Which operation combines all elements from two sets (without duplicates)?
quiz.e: Union combines elements from both sets into one, removing duplicates.

quiz.e: The root is the topmost node from which all other nodes descend.

quiz.q: What is a binary tree?
o: A tree where each node has at most two children
A tree with only one node
A tree stored in binary code
quiz.e: In a binary tree, each node has at most two children, often called left and right.

quiz.q: What is a graph, in data structure terms?
o: A structure of nodes (vertices) connected by edges, representing relationships
quiz.e: Graphs model nodes and the connections (edges) between them, useful for networks.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a directed and undirected graph?
o: Directed edges go one way; undirected edges go both ways
quiz.e: Directed graph edges have a specific direction; undirected edges can be traversed both ways.

quiz.q: Which data structure would best model 'undo' functionality in a text editor?
quiz.e: A stack naturally supports undoing the most recent action first (LIFO).

quiz.q: Which data structure would best model a line of customers waiting to be served in order?
quiz.e: A queue processes items (customers) in the order they arrived (FIFO).

quiz.q: Which data structure would best store unique usernames and quickly check if one is already taken?
quiz.e: A set efficiently enforces uniqueness and supports fast membership checks.

quiz.q: Which data structure would best store a phone book mapping names to phone numbers?
quiz.e: A dictionary maps each name (key) to a phone number (value) for fast lookup.

quiz.q: What generally makes dictionary/hash map lookups fast?
o: They store data in alphabetical order only
A hash function converts the key into an internal index
They search every entry one at a time
quiz.e: Hashing computes a direct index from the key, avoiding a full search.

quiz.q: What is a 2D array commonly used to represent?
o: A grid, like a spreadsheet or game board
quiz.e: A 2D array (array of arrays) naturally models rows and columns, like a grid.

quiz.q: Which best describes a 'leaf' node in a tree?
o: A node with exactly two children
quiz.e: A leaf node is at the end of a branch and has no children.

quiz.q: Why might searching for a specific value in an unsorted array be slower than a dictionary lookup?
o: An unsorted array may require checking each element one by one, while a dictionary can jump directly via hashing
Dictionaries are always smaller in size
There is no actual difference in speed
quiz.e: Linear search through an unsorted array can require checking every element, while hashing gives near-direct access.

quiz.q: What best distinguishes a tree from a general graph?
o: Trees cannot have more than one node
A tree is a special graph with one root and no cycles
Trees always have exactly two children per node
quiz.e: A tree is a hierarchical graph with a single root, no cycles, and each node connected via exactly one path from the root.

quiz.q: What happens when you add a value to a set that it already contains?
o: The set is unaffected since it only stores unique values
The set converts to a list
quiz.e: Sets ignore duplicate additions since they only hold unique values.

quiz.q: What is the 'difference' operation between two sets, A and B (A - B)?
o: Elements in both A and B
Elements in A that are not in B
Elements in neither A nor B
quiz.e: A - B returns elements present in A but not in B.

quiz.q: Which data structure allows accessing elements by both index (position) and does not require unique values?
quiz.e: Arrays/lists support duplicate values and direct index-based access.

quiz.q: What is an 'edge' in a graph or tree?
quiz.e: An edge represents the connection/relationship between two nodes.

quiz.q: Why are stacks useful for tracking function calls in a program (the 'call stack')?
o: Functions must run in random order
The most recently called function needs to finish and return first, matching LIFO behavior
Function calls never need to be tracked
Stacks are only used for numbers
quiz.e: Since the most recent function call must complete before returning to the previous one, a stack's LIFO order fits naturally.

quiz.q: Which is generally true about dictionary key-value pairs?
o: Values must be unique but keys can repeat
Keys must be unique but values can repeat
Both keys and values must be unique
quiz.e: Dictionary keys must be unique for lookups to work unambiguously, but values may repeat.

quiz.q: What data structure would be most efficient for scheduling print jobs in the order they were submitted?
quiz.e: A queue processes jobs FIFO, matching the order they were submitted.

quiz.q: What kind of tree would you use to organize a company's reporting hierarchy?
o: A binary tree strictly limited to 2 children
A general tree, since managers may have many direct reports
quiz.e: A general tree allows any number of children per node, fitting an org chart better than a strict binary tree.

quiz.q: What does it mean that arrays have a 'fixed size' in some languages?
o: Once created, the array cannot grow or shrink without creating a new one
quiz.e: In some languages, arrays are allocated at a fixed size and cannot be resized directly.

quiz.q: Which best explains why Python lists differ slightly from traditional fixed-size arrays?
o: Python lists cannot store multiple types
Python lists can dynamically grow and shrink as elements are added or removed
quiz.e: Python's built-in list type is dynamic, automatically resizing as needed.

quiz.q: What is a practical example of using a stack in web browsers?
o: The 'back' button history, since the most recently visited page is revisited first
quiz.e: Browser back-button history behaves like a stack, returning to the most recently visited page first.

quiz.q: Which statement about hashing and collisions is most accurate?
o: Two different keys can never produce the same hash-based index
Collisions (two keys mapping to the same index) can occur and hash maps have strategies to handle them
Hashing is only used for security, never for data structures
Collisions always break the whole hash map
quiz.e: Hash maps use collision-handling strategies (like chaining) because different keys can occasionally map to the same index.

quiz.q: Which structure would be most natural for representing nested folders and files on a computer?
quiz.e: A file system's nested folder structure is naturally modeled as a tree, with folders as parent nodes.

quiz.q: When would choosing a set over a list be most beneficial?
o: When order and duplicates both matter
When you need fast membership checks and don't care about duplicates or order
When you need to access items by numeric index
quiz.e: Sets excel at fast 'is this value present?' checks and automatically discarding duplicates.

quiz.q: What best distinguishes push/pop operations from enqueue/dequeue operations?
o: They are identical operations with different names
Push/pop operate on a stack (LIFO); enqueue/dequeue operate on a queue (FIFO)
quiz.e: Push/pop describe stack operations, while enqueue/dequeue describe queue operations, reflecting their different orderings.

quiz.q: What is an algorithm?
o: A precise, step-by-step procedure for solving a problem
quiz.e: An algorithm is a clear, ordered sequence of steps to solve a problem.

quiz.q: What must an algorithm do, unlike a potentially infinite loop?
quiz.e: A valid algorithm must eventually reach an end, unlike a runaway infinite loop.

quiz.q: What is pseudocode?
o: An informal, human-readable way to outline an algorithm before coding it
quiz.e: Pseudocode describes algorithm logic in plain, structured language without strict syntax.

quiz.q: What is required before performing a binary search on a collection?
o: The collection must be a dictionary
The collection must contain only numbers
quiz.e: Binary search relies on the data being sorted to correctly eliminate halves.

quiz.q: How does binary search find a target value?
o: It checks every element in order from the start
It repeatedly checks the middle element and eliminates half the remaining data
It sorts the data first every time it's called
quiz.e: Binary search compares the middle element and discards the half that can't contain the target.

quiz.q: What is the main limitation of linear search compared to binary search on large datasets?
o: Linear search requires sorted data; binary search does not
Linear search can be much slower since it may check every element
Linear search cannot be used on arrays
Linear search always fails on large datasets
quiz.e: Linear search's worst case checks every item, making it slower than binary search for large sorted datasets.

quiz.q: What Big-O notation describes constant time complexity?
quiz.e: O(1) means the operation takes the same time regardless of input size.

quiz.q: What Big-O notation describes linear time complexity?
quiz.e: O(n) means runtime grows proportionally with input size.

quiz.q: What Big-O notation typically describes binary search's efficiency?
quiz.e: Binary search runs in O(log n) time because it halves the search space each step.

quiz.q: What Big-O notation typically describes bubble sort's efficiency?
quiz.e: Bubble sort's nested comparisons over the data give it O(n²) time in typical/worst cases.

quiz.q: How does bubble sort work?
o: It divides data in half repeatedly
It repeatedly compares adjacent elements and swaps them if out of order
It uses a hash function to sort
It only works on sorted data
quiz.e: Bubble sort makes multiple passes, swapping adjacent out-of-order elements each time.

quiz.q: What describes the general approach of merge sort?
o: Divide the data in half repeatedly, sort each half, then merge the sorted halves
quiz.e: Merge sort is a divide-and-conquer algorithm: split, sort recursively, then merge.

quiz.q: Why is Big-O notation useful for comparing algorithms?
o: It gives an exact number of seconds on any computer
It describes how runtime/memory use grows with input size, independent of hardware
It only applies to sorting algorithms
It measures how much electricity an algorithm uses
quiz.e: Big-O abstracts away hardware specifics to describe growth trends as input size increases.

quiz.q: What is 'decomposition' as a problem-solving strategy?
o: Breaking a large problem into smaller, more manageable subproblems
quiz.e: Decomposition splits complex problems into simpler pieces that are easier to solve individually.

quiz.q: What is 'abstraction' in problem solving?
o: Focusing on important details while ignoring irrelevant complexity
quiz.e: Abstraction simplifies a problem by hiding unnecessary detail and focusing on what matters.

quiz.q: Why should you test an algorithm with edge cases, like empty input?
o: Edge cases often expose problems that typical inputs do not
Testing is unnecessary if the algorithm compiles
Edge cases only matter for sorting algorithms
quiz.e: Boundary/edge cases frequently reveal issues a typical test case might miss.

quiz.q: What does it generally mean when one algorithm has a 'time versus space trade-off' compared to another?
o: It can only run on certain hardware
It might run faster while using more memory, or vice versa
It always uses less of both time and memory
quiz.e: Some algorithms trade increased memory use for faster runtime, or vice versa.

quiz.q: For a very small input size, why might a simple O(n²) algorithm be acceptable in practice?
o: The difference in actual runtime may be negligible for small inputs
O(n²) is always faster than O(n) for any size
Simple algorithms are always the fastest
quiz.e: Growth-rate differences matter most for large inputs; for small inputs the practical time difference can be minimal.

quiz.q: What happens to the runtime of an O(n²) algorithm if the input size doubles?
