quiz.e: Quadratic growth means doubling input size roughly quadruples the work (2² = 4).

quiz.q: What happens to the runtime of an O(log n) algorithm as input size grows very large?
o: It grows very slowly, since each step cuts the problem in half
quiz.e: Logarithmic growth increases very slowly because the problem size is repeatedly halved.

quiz.q: Which best describes selection sort?
o: It repeatedly finds the smallest remaining element and places it in order
It only works on linked lists
quiz.e: Selection sort selects the minimum remaining element each pass and moves it into place.

quiz.q: Why must an algorithm's steps be unambiguous?
o: So a computer can follow them exactly without needing to guess intent
To make the algorithm harder to understand
quiz.e: Since computers can't infer intent, each instruction must have one precise, clear meaning.

quiz.q: Which of these best illustrates a real-world use of binary search?
o: Looking up a word in a dictionary by flipping to a rough midpoint and narrowing down
Reading a book cover to cover
Randomly opening pages until you find the word
quiz.e: Flipping to an estimated midpoint and narrowing the range mirrors binary search's halving strategy.

quiz.q: Why is sorting often a prerequisite for using binary search efficiently?
o: Binary search works equally well on unsorted data
Binary search's halving logic depends on the data being in order to correctly discard halves
Sorting has nothing to do with searching
Binary search doesn't require any particular data organization
quiz.e: Without a sorted order, you cannot reliably determine which half contains the target.

quiz.q: What is the worst-case time complexity generally associated with linear search?
quiz.e: In the worst case, linear search must check every one of the n elements.

quiz.q: What does drawing a flowchart before coding typically help with?
o: Making the final code run faster automatically
Visually planning the logic and flow of a solution before implementation
quiz.e: Flowcharts and diagrams help plan and visualize logic before writing actual code.

quiz.q: Which statement about algorithm correctness is most accurate?
o: An algorithm is correct if it works on one sample input
An algorithm should be verified to work for all valid inputs, not just given examples
Correctness cannot be tested, only assumed
quiz.e: True correctness requires the algorithm to handle all valid inputs, not just the examples you tried.

quiz.q: Why might merge sort be preferred over bubble sort for large datasets?
o: Merge sort is always simpler to write
Merge sort's divide-and-conquer approach scales much better (typically O(n log n)) than bubble sort's O(n²)
There is no meaningful performance difference
quiz.e: Merge sort's better growth rate makes it far more efficient than bubble sort as data size increases.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of looking for patterns or similar previously-solved problems when problem solving?
o: It guarantees an immediate solution with zero effort
It can save time by reusing known strategies or algorithms that fit the new problem
Patterns are irrelevant to computer science
It only works for sorting problems
quiz.e: Recognizing a problem resembles one already solved lets you apply or adapt a known algorithm.

quiz.q: Which best explains why 'good enough and correct' is often favored over 'theoretically fastest but error-prone' in real engineering?
o: A slower but reliable, well-understood solution often provides more overall value than a faster but buggy or hard-to-maintain one
Fast algorithms are always simple to implement correctly
Efficiency is never a practical concern
quiz.e: Correctness, maintainability, and reliability often outweigh marginal theoretical speed gains in practice.

quiz.q: If an array is unsorted, what must typically happen before an efficient binary search can be used?
o: Nothing; binary search works on any data
The array must first be sorted
The array must be converted to a dictionary
The array must be doubled in size
quiz.e: Binary search requires sorted input to correctly narrow down the search range.

quiz.q: Which best describes the relationship between an algorithm and a specific programming language?
o: An algorithm can only be described in one specific programming language
An algorithm is a language-independent set of steps that could be implemented in many programming languages
Algorithms and programming languages are the same thing
Pseudocode is a real, executable programming language
quiz.e: An algorithm describes the logic of a solution abstractly, separate from any one language's syntax.

quiz.q: Why does testing with 'simple cases first, then edge cases' make sense as a strategy?
o: It verifies basic correctness before checking tricky boundary conditions that often reveal bugs
Edge cases should always be tested before simple cases
Simple cases are irrelevant to correctness
quiz.e: Confirming the basic logic works first, then probing edge cases, helps isolate where issues arise.

quiz.q: What best distinguishes O(n) from O(n²) in practical terms for very large n?
o: O(n²) grows much faster than O(n), often becoming impractically slow for large n
O(n) is always slower than O(n²)
Neither notation relates to actual performance
quiz.e: Quadratic growth (O(n²)) scales far worse than linear growth (O(n)) as input size increases.

quiz.q: What is a key reason binary search is considered more efficient than linear search for large sorted datasets?
o: It checks fewer elements by eliminating half the remaining data each step
It doesn't need the data to be in memory
It always finds the answer in one step
quiz.e: By discarding half the remaining elements each comparison, binary search needs far fewer steps than checking one by one.

quiz.q: What is the best-case scenario for linear search?
o: The target is the very first element checked
The target is always the last element
The list must be sorted first
quiz.e: If the target is the first element, linear search finds it immediately, in O(1) time for that case.

quiz.q: Which sorting algorithm approach is described as 'divide and conquer'?
quiz.e: Merge sort divides the problem into halves, solves each recursively, then combines (conquers) the results.

quiz.q: Why is it important for pseudocode to be written before actual code?
o: Pseudocode replaces the need for testing
It helps clarify and plan the logic of a solution in a language-independent way before dealing with syntax
Pseudocode is required by all compilers
Pseudocode always runs faster than real code
quiz.e: Pseudocode lets you focus on logic and structure without worrying about a specific language's syntax rules.

quiz.q: If input size n increases from 10 to 100, how does an O(n) algorithm's runtime roughly change?
quiz.e: Linear growth means runtime scales proportionally with input size, so a 10x increase in n gives roughly 10x more work.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT typically a step in a good problem-solving process?
o: Skipping testing once code compiles without errors
quiz.e: Compiling without errors only confirms valid syntax — testing for correct behavior, including edge cases, is still essential.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between the internet and the World Wide Web?
o: They are exactly the same thing
The internet is the network infrastructure; the Web is a system of linked documents that runs on it
The Web existed before the internet
The internet only refers to email
quiz.e: The internet is the underlying network; the Web is one service/application that uses it.

quiz.q: What does an IP address do?
o: Uniquely identifies a device on a network
quiz.e: An IP address is a numeric label that identifies a device on a network.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of DNS (Domain Name System)?
o: To translate human-readable domain names into numeric IP addresses
quiz.e: DNS converts names like example.com into the IP addresses computers actually use to connect.

quiz.q: What is HTTP?
o: The protocol browsers and servers use to communicate requests and responses
quiz.e: HTTP defines the rules for how web clients and servers exchange information.

quiz.q: What does HTTPS add compared to plain HTTP?
o: Encryption of data in transit via SSL/TLS
quiz.e: HTTPS secures the connection by encrypting data between browser and server.

quiz.q: What does a 404 HTTP status code indicate?
o: The requested resource was not found
quiz.e: 404 means the server couldn't find the resource at the requested URL.

quiz.q: What does a 200 HTTP status code indicate?
quiz.e: 200 OK indicates the request was processed successfully.

quiz.q: What does a 500 HTTP status code indicate?
o: An error occurred on the server's side while processing the request
quiz.e: 500 Internal Server Error signals a problem on the server, not the client.

quiz.q: What is HTML primarily used for?
o: Structuring a webpage's content, like headings and paragraphs
quiz.e: HTML provides the structural markup (tags) that defines webpage content.

quiz.q: What is CSS primarily used for?
o: Controlling a webpage's visual presentation, like colors and layout
quiz.e: CSS handles the visual styling of HTML content.

quiz.q: What is JavaScript primarily used for on a webpage?
o: Adding interactivity and dynamic behavior to a webpage
quiz.e: JavaScript is a programming language that runs in the browser to make pages interactive.

quiz.q: What is the role of a 'client' in a client-server model?
o: It stores and provides resources to others
It requests resources or services, typically via a browser or app
It replaces the need for a server
quiz.e: The client (e.g., a web browser) sends requests to a server for resources.

quiz.q: What is the role of a 'server' in a client-server model?
o: It stores data/resources and responds to client requests
It only displays content to users
quiz.e: A server stores resources and responds to client requests, such as serving a webpage.

quiz.q: What is a URL?
o: An address specifying the location of a resource, including protocol, domain, and path
quiz.e: A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) is the full address used to locate a specific resource online.

quiz.q: Which HTTP method is typically used to retrieve data from a server?
quiz.e: GET requests are used to retrieve (fetch) data without modifying it.

quiz.q: Which HTTP method is typically used to submit new data to a server?
quiz.e: POST requests typically send/submit new data to be processed by the server.

quiz.q: What are cookies, in the context of web browsing?
o: Small pieces of data a server asks the browser to store, often for sessions or preferences
quiz.e: Cookies let servers remember information about a user across requests, like login state.

quiz.q: What is a firewall used for?
o: Monitoring and controlling network traffic based on security rules
Translating domain names to IP addresses
quiz.e: Firewalls filter network traffic to block unauthorized or harmful connections.

quiz.q: What does encryption do to data?
o: Scrambles it so only someone with the correct key can read it
Compresses it to save space only
quiz.e: Encryption transforms readable data into a scrambled form that requires a key to decode.

quiz.q: What is bandwidth?
o: The physical size of a router
A measure of how much data can be transferred over a connection in a given time
The number of devices on a network
quiz.e: Bandwidth measures data transfer capacity over a network connection, often in bits per second.

quiz.q: Why is public Wi-Fi generally considered riskier than a private home network?
o: Data on shared public networks may be more easily intercepted by others
Public Wi-Fi uses a different, safer protocol
There is no actual difference in risk
quiz.e: Open or shared networks can make it easier for others to intercept unencrypted traffic.

quiz.q: What does 'front-end' web development generally focus on?
o: What users see and interact with directly in the browser
quiz.e: Front-end development covers the client-side experience: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript in the browser.

quiz.q: What does 'back-end' web development generally focus on?
o: Servers, databases, and logic running behind the scenes
quiz.e: Back-end development handles server-side logic, databases, and infrastructure.

quiz.q: What is a packet, in networking terms?
o: A small chunk of data that travels across a network and is reassembled at the destination
quiz.e: Data is broken into packets for efficient transmission and reassembled upon arrival.

quiz.q: Why was IPv6 developed?
o: IPv4 addresses were running out as more devices connected to the internet
IPv6 is only used for email
quiz.e: The limited number of IPv4 addresses couldn't keep up with the growing number of internet-connected devices.

quiz.q: What best describes the relationship between a domain name and DNS?
o: A domain name is stored inside cookies only
DNS translates a domain name into the IP address needed to locate the actual server
Domain names replace the need for IP addresses entirely
DNS and domain names are unrelated
quiz.e: DNS resolves the human-friendly domain name to the numeric IP address of the hosting server.

quiz.q: Which best explains why HTTPS uses SSL/TLS?
o: To make webpages load without any content
To encrypt data exchanged between browser and server, protecting it from interception
To replace domain names with IP addresses
quiz.e: SSL/TLS provides the encryption layer that HTTPS uses to secure communication.

quiz.q: What is the internet best described as?
o: A 'network of networks' connecting devices worldwide
quiz.e: The internet is a vast, interconnected system of many individual networks working together.

quiz.q: If a webpage fails to load and shows a 404 error, what does this suggest?
o: The specific requested resource/page could not be found at that address
The user's computer has a virus
quiz.e: A 404 is specific to the requested URL, not a sign of a broader internet outage.

quiz.q: Which of the following best distinguishes HTML, CSS, and JavaScript?
o: They all do the exact same job
HTML structures content, CSS styles it, and JavaScript adds interactive behavior
CSS structures content, HTML styles it, JavaScript is optional
JavaScript replaces the need for HTML and CSS entirely
quiz.e: Each of the three technologies plays a distinct, complementary role in building webpages.

quiz.q: What might cause a website to show a 500 error but not a 404 error?
o: The URL is valid, but something failed on the server while processing the request
The user's internet connection is off
quiz.e: 500 indicates the server found the resource/route but encountered an internal problem while handling it.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a router in a home network?
o: To connect devices within a local network and link that network to the wider internet
To encrypt files on a hard drive
quiz.e: A router directs traffic between devices on a local network and out to the internet.

quiz.q: Which best describes why the internet has 'no single owner'?
o: It's illegal to own the internet
It operates through many cooperating networks following shared standard protocols, rather than one central authority
Governments jointly own all internet infrastructure
Only one company controls global internet traffic
quiz.e: The internet functions through decentralized, cooperating networks agreeing to common protocols.

quiz.q: Why might a website use cookies to remember a logged-in user?
o: Cookies are required by law for all websites
Cookies let the server recognize returning requests as part of the same session without re-entering credentials each time
Cookies replace the need for a server entirely
Cookies only work with HTTPS, never HTTP
quiz.e: Session cookies allow a server to track logged-in state across multiple requests from the same browser.

quiz.q: Which best describes what happens when you type a URL into a browser and press enter?
o: The browser immediately displays cached data with no network activity
The browser resolves the domain via DNS, sends an HTTP(S) request to the server, and renders the returned content
The computer converts the URL into binary and stops there
Nothing happens until you refresh the page
quiz.e: Loading a page involves DNS resolution, an HTTP(S) request/response cycle, and rendering the received content.

quiz.q: Which HTTP method is typically used to remove a resource from a server?
quiz.e: DELETE requests ask the server to remove the specified resource.

quiz.q: What is a 'network', in general computing terms?
o: Any group of connected devices that can share data
quiz.e: A network is a set of interconnected devices capable of exchanging data.

quiz.q: Why does DNS make the internet easier for humans to use?
o: It removes the need for servers
It lets people use memorable names instead of numeric IP addresses
It encrypts all web traffic automatically
It replaces HTTP with a faster protocol
quiz.e: DNS lets users type easy-to-remember domain names instead of numeric IP addresses.

quiz.q: What best describes the format of a typical IPv4 address?
o: Four numbers 0-255 separated by dots, like 192.168.1.1
quiz.e: IPv4 addresses consist of four dot-separated numbers, each ranging from 0 to 255.

quiz.q: Which best explains why a domain name might point to a different IP address over time?
o: Domain names never change their target
Servers or hosting providers can change, and DNS records are updated to reflect the new IP address
IP addresses never change once assigned
quiz.e: DNS records can be updated so a domain name resolves to a new server's IP address when hosting changes.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between encryption and hashing?
o: Encryption is reversible with a key; hashing is one-way and cannot be reversed
Hashing is reversible; encryption is not
They are the same process with different names
Encryption only works on text; hashing only works on numbers
quiz.e: Encryption is designed to be decrypted with the correct key; hashing intentionally produces a one-way transformation used for verification, not recovery.

quiz.q: In symmetric encryption, what is used to both encrypt and decrypt data?
quiz.e: Symmetric encryption uses one shared key for both encrypting and decrypting, which makes it fast but requires securely distributing that key.

quiz.q: How does asymmetric encryption differ from symmetric encryption?
o: It uses a public key to encrypt and a private key to decrypt
It uses no keys at all
It is always faster than symmetric encryption
It cannot be used for secure web browsing
quiz.e: Asymmetric encryption uses a mathematically linked key pair: anyone can encrypt with the public key, but only the private key holder can decrypt.

quiz.q: Why does HTTPS use both asymmetric and symmetric encryption?
o: Asymmetric encryption safely exchanges a session key, then symmetric encryption efficiently protects the ongoing data
Symmetric encryption is used only for the padlock icon
Asymmetric encryption is used for the entire session because it is faster
HTTPS does not use encryption at all
quiz.e: Asymmetric encryption is slower but solves key exchange safely; the resulting shared key is then used with fast symmetric encryption for the actual traffic.

quiz.q: What does the padlock icon in a browser actually guarantee?
o: The website is completely trustworthy and safe
The connection between browser and server is encrypted
The website has no tracking cookies
The website has passed a government security audit
quiz.e: The padlock only indicates an encrypted (HTTPS/TLS) connection — it says nothing about whether the site's owner or content is trustworthy.

quiz.q: Which of these is a common cause of data breaches?
o: Phishing attacks that steal login credentials
quiz.e: Phishing tricks users into handing over credentials directly, making it one of the most common breach vectors, alongside unpatched software and weak passwords.

quiz.q: Why do companies hash and salt stored passwords?
o: So a stolen password database doesn't reveal usable plaintext passwords
To make passwords load faster on login pages
Because hashing is required by web browsers
To make passwords easier for employees to read
quiz.e: Hashing (with salting) ensures that even if attackers steal the password database, they cannot easily recover the original passwords.

quiz.q: What problem does two-factor authentication (2FA) solve?
o: It prevents login even if a password alone is stolen
It encrypts all of a user's files automatically
It blocks all phishing emails before they arrive
quiz.e: 2FA requires a second proof of identity (like a code sent to a phone), so a stolen password alone isn't enough to access the account.

quiz.q: What is credential stuffing?
o: Trying stolen username/password pairs from one breach on other websites
A method for generating strong random passwords
quiz.e: Credential stuffing exploits password reuse: attackers take credentials leaked from one breach and try them on many other sites.

quiz.q: What is the main risk of reusing the same password across multiple sites?
o: It slows down your internet connection
A breach at one site can be used to access your accounts elsewhere
It uses more storage space on your device
quiz.e: If one site is breached, attackers can reuse the exposed password (via credential stuffing) to log into your other accounts that share it.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a first-party and third-party cookie?
o: First-party cookies are set by the site you're visiting; third-party cookies are set by other embedded domains
There is no functional difference between them
Third-party cookies are always more secure
First-party cookies can only store passwords
quiz.e: First-party cookies come from the site you're on (e.g. keeping you logged in); third-party cookies come from other domains embedded on the page, often ad networks.

quiz.q: How do third-party cookies enable cross-site tracking?
o: They physically transfer files between computers
The same tracker can see visits to many different sites and build a behavior profile
They only work on government websites
They delete themselves after every page load
quiz.e: Because the same ad network's cookie can be embedded on many sites, it can recognize the same browser across all of them and build a tracking profile.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a session cookie and a persistent cookie?
o: Session cookies expire when the browser closes; persistent cookies last until a set expiration date
Persistent cookies expire instantly; session cookies never expire
They are identical in every way
Session cookies can only store images
quiz.e: Session cookies are temporary and clear when you close the browser, while persistent cookies remain stored until they expire or are manually deleted.

quiz.q: Why have browsers moved to block third-party cookies by default?
o: To speed up page loading only
To limit cross-site tracking of users by advertisers
Because third-party cookies are illegal everywhere
To force websites to remove all cookies
quiz.e: Blocking third-party cookies is primarily a privacy measure aimed at reducing advertisers' ability to track users across unrelated websites.

quiz.q: What does clearing your browser's cookies actually accomplish?
o: It permanently deletes all data companies have already collected about you
It logs you out of sites and removes locally stored tracking history
It prevents any future website from ever tracking you
quiz.e: Clearing cookies removes what's stored locally (login sessions, local tracking data) but does not erase data trackers already collected and stored on their own servers.

quiz.q: Under GDPR, what is the 'right to erasure'?
o: The right to demand a company delete your personal data
The right to erase a company's public reviews
The right to unlimited free storage
The right to erase other users' data
quiz.e: The right to erasure, or 'right to be forgotten,' lets individuals request that an organization delete the personal data it holds about them.

quiz.q: What does 'data minimization' mean under privacy regulations like GDPR?
o: Collecting as much data as possible for future use
Collecting only the data actually necessary for a stated purpose
Storing data on the smallest possible hard drive
Minimizing the number of employees who can access data centers
quiz.e: Data minimization requires organizations to limit collection to what's genuinely needed for the purpose they've disclosed, not gather everything possible 'just in case.'

quiz.q: Under GDPR, how quickly must a company report a data breach to regulators?
o: Only if fewer than 10 users are affected
quiz.e: GDPR requires organizations to notify the relevant regulator of a data breach within 72 hours of becoming aware of it.

quiz.q: Why do many non-EU websites still show GDPR-style cookie consent banners?
o: GDPR applies to any company handling EU residents' data, regardless of where the company is based
It is purely a design trend with no legal basis
All websites are legally required to show ads
Cookie banners are unrelated to any privacy law
quiz.e: GDPR's scope covers the personal data of EU residents no matter where the processing company is located, so global sites comply to serve EU visitors.

quiz.q: What is phishing?
o: A social engineering attack that impersonates a trusted source to steal credentials
A method of speeding up network traffic
quiz.e: Phishing exploits human trust by impersonating a legitimate sender (bank, coworker, service) to trick victims into revealing credentials or installing malware.

quiz.q: What distinguishes ransomware from other malware types?
o: It encrypts a victim's files and demands payment for the decryption key
It speeds up a computer's performance
It is not considered malicious software
quiz.e: Ransomware specifically locks victims out of their own data by encrypting it, then demands payment (a ransom) for the key to decrypt it.

quiz.q: What is the role of a firewall in cybersecurity?
o: It filters network traffic based on security rules to block unauthorized access
It encrypts all files on a hard drive automatically
It generates random passwords for users
It permanently deletes malware from a system
quiz.e: A firewall inspects incoming and outgoing network traffic against defined rules, blocking traffic that looks unauthorized while allowing legitimate traffic through.

quiz.q: What is the 'principle of least privilege'?
o: Giving every user full administrator access for convenience
Giving users and programs only the access they need to perform their task
Removing all access controls from a system
Only applying security rules to executives
quiz.e: Least privilege limits each account or process to the minimum access required, so a compromised account causes less damage.

quiz.q: Why is social engineering considered a major cybersecurity threat despite not exploiting technical flaws?
o: It exploits human trust and behavior rather than software vulnerabilities
It only affects outdated computer hardware
It cannot be used to steal any real information
It requires physical access to every target device
quiz.e: Social engineering bypasses technical defenses entirely by manipulating people directly, which is why user awareness training is a critical complement to technical security.

quiz.q: Why is delaying software updates a security risk?
o: Updates often fix known vulnerabilities that attackers can already exploit
Updates have no effect on system security
Older software is always more secure than newer software
quiz.e: Patches frequently close known security holes; once a vulnerability is public, unpatched systems become easy, well-documented targets.

quiz.q: What is a worm, in the context of malware?
o: Malware that self-replicates and spreads across networks without needing a host file
A hardware component used to filter traffic
A privacy regulation similar to GDPR
quiz.e: Unlike a virus, which attaches to files, a worm can spread on its own across a network, exploiting vulnerabilities to replicate.

quiz.q: Why is device fingerprinting a growing tracking method?
o: It requires cookies to be enabled to function at all
It identifies devices by unique settings/hardware traits, working even as third-party cookies decline
It replaces the need for encryption
quiz.e: As browsers block third-party cookies, advertisers increasingly rely on fingerprinting — combining browser/device characteristics — to keep identifying users across sites.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of requiring 'informed consent' for data collection under privacy law?
o: To make sure users clearly understand and agree to what data is collected and why
To let companies collect data without limits as long as a banner appears
To eliminate the need for any privacy policy
To speed up website loading times
quiz.e: Informed consent means users must be clearly told what's collected and why, and must actively agree — pre-checked boxes or buried terms don't satisfy this.

quiz.q: Which scenario best illustrates a data breach?
o: A user updates their own password voluntarily
An attacker exploits an unpatched server flaw to download a customer database
A company deletes old customer records per its retention policy
A user enables two-factor authentication on their account
quiz.e: A breach involves unauthorized access to data — here, an attacker exploiting a vulnerability to steal a database is a textbook example.

quiz.q: What should a company do first after discovering a data breach?
o: Ignore it if fewer than 100 users are affected
Patch the vulnerability, notify affected users/regulators, and force password resets
Wait a year before telling anyone
quiz.e: Responsible breach response includes closing the security hole, notifying those affected and required regulators, and prompting credential resets to limit damage.

quiz.q: Why can outdated encryption algorithms become insecure over time?
o: Increasing computing power makes brute-force attacks against them feasible
Old algorithms stop working on new computers entirely
Encryption algorithms expire automatically after a fixed date
Outdated algorithms use no keys at all
quiz.e: As computing power grows, algorithms once considered secure (like older DES) become crackable through brute force, which is why standards evolve toward stronger ones like AES.

quiz.q: A shopping site remembers your cart items after you navigate to another page on the same site. What is most likely responsible?
quiz.e: Remembering cart contents across pages on the same site is a classic first-party cookie use case — it's set and read by the site you're actually using.

quiz.q: What makes salting passwords more secure than hashing alone?
o: Salting makes identical passwords produce different hashes, defeating precomputed lookup-table attacks
Salting encrypts the password so it can be reversed later
Salting removes the need for hashing entirely
Salting only works on numeric passwords
quiz.e: Without a salt, identical passwords hash to identical values, letting attackers use precomputed tables; a unique random salt per password defeats that shortcut.

quiz.q: Which best explains why HTTPS matters for entering a credit card number online?
o: It encrypts the data in transit so it can't be easily intercepted and read by eavesdroppers
It guarantees the merchant will not be hacked later
It automatically enrolls you in fraud protection
It replaces the need for a strong password
quiz.e: HTTPS protects data as it travels between your browser and the server, preventing eavesdroppers on the network from reading sensitive information like card numbers.

quiz.q: Why might a company be fined heavily under GDPR for a violation?
o: Fines are calculated as a percentage of global revenue, which can be very large for big companies
GDPR fines are always a fixed $10 regardless of company size
GDPR does not include any financial penalties
Fines only apply to individuals, never companies
quiz.e: GDPR penalties scale with a company's global annual revenue, which is designed to make noncompliance costly even for the largest corporations.

quiz.q: What is one key limitation of relying only on a firewall for security?
o: It cannot stop attacks that trick users directly, like phishing or social engineering
It makes all software updates unnecessary
It automatically encrypts every file on the network
It eliminates the need for strong passwords
quiz.e: A firewall filters network traffic but can't prevent a user from being tricked into handing over credentials directly, which is why layered defenses are needed.

quiz.q: Why is it misleading to think of encryption and privacy laws as solving the same problem?
o: Encryption is a technical tool protecting data confidentiality; privacy law governs how organizations may collect, use, and share data
They are functionally identical and interchangeable
Privacy laws only apply to encrypted data
Encryption automatically ensures full legal compliance
quiz.e: Encryption is a technical safeguard against unauthorized access to data, whereas privacy regulation addresses the separate question of what data may be collected and how it may be used, regardless of encryption.

quiz.q: Which practice best reduces the impact of a future data breach on an individual user?
o: Using the same strong password across every account for consistency
Using unique passwords per site plus two-factor authentication
Avoiding software updates to reduce compatibility issues
quiz.e: Unique passwords limit the blast radius of any single breach, and 2FA adds a barrier even if a password is exposed — together they're the most effective personal defense.

quiz.q: A website's privacy policy says it collects your location, contacts, and browsing history to 'improve services,' none of which relate to its stated function as a note-taking app. What principle does this likely violate?
quiz.e: Collecting far more data than needed for the app's actual purpose violates the data minimization principle central to privacy regulations like GDPR.

quiz.q: What is the practical difference between a virus and a worm?
o: A virus needs a host file to attach to and spread; a worm can self-replicate across a network independently
A virus only affects mobile devices; a worm only affects desktops
They are the same thing with different names
A worm is a defensive tool, while a virus is offensive
quiz.e: Viruses require a carrier file and often user action to spread, while worms can propagate autonomously across networked systems by exploiting vulnerabilities.

quiz.q: Why do security experts recommend against clicking links in unexpected emails asking you to 'verify your account'?
o: Such emails are always sent by search engines
This is a common phishing tactic used to steal login credentials
Clicking links always installs antivirus software
quiz.e: Urgent 'verify your account' emails with links are a hallmark phishing tactic designed to lead victims to fake login pages that harvest their credentials.

quiz.q: What is the most common root cause of algorithmic bias?
quiz.e: Most algorithmic bias emerges unintentionally from training data that reflects historical or societal bias, not from explicit discriminatory intent.

quiz.q: Why might a hiring algorithm trained on a company's past resumes produce biased results?
o: It will always be perfectly fair since it uses real data
It can learn to favor whatever demographics were historically hired, replicating past bias
Algorithms cannot use resume data at all
It automatically corrects for any historical bias
quiz.e: If past hiring decisions were biased, a model trained on that history can learn and reproduce the same patterns, even without being told to consider demographics.

quiz.q: What is a proxy variable in the context of algorithmic bias?
o: A feature that indirectly encodes a sensitive attribute through correlation, like zip code standing in for race
A backup variable used only when a program crashes
A synonym for a randomly generated number
quiz.e: Proxy variables let sensitive information leak into a model indirectly — zip code, for instance, can correlate strongly with race even if race itself is excluded.

quiz.q: Why doesn't removing a sensitive attribute like race from a dataset guarantee a fair model?
o: Because correlated proxy variables can still encode that same information indirectly
Because removing any column makes a model automatically less accurate
Because sensitive attributes cannot be removed by law
Because fairness is not affected by data at all
quiz.e: Other features correlated with the removed attribute (proxies) can still let the model reconstruct and act on that sensitive information.

quiz.q: What is a feedback loop in the context of a biased predictive model?
o: A situation where a model's biased outputs generate new data that reinforces the original bias over time
A hardware component that improves processing speed
A method for encrypting model outputs
A required step in every open-source license
quiz.e: For example, a predictive policing model that over-patrols a neighborhood generates more arrests there, which is then used as 'evidence' to justify even more patrols — amplifying the original bias.

quiz.q: What does 'disparate impact' mean when auditing an algorithm?
o: A policy or algorithm that appears neutral but produces significantly worse outcomes for one group
A measure of how fast a model runs
The total number of users affected by a system
A type of software license violation
quiz.e: Disparate impact analysis checks whether an outwardly neutral system's real-world outcomes are actually unequal across different groups.

quiz.q: Why is overall model accuracy alone not enough to prove a system is fair?
o: Accuracy is impossible to measure in AI systems
A model can have high overall accuracy while performing far worse for specific subgroups
Accuracy always guarantees fairness across all groups
Fairness is a purely legal concept unrelated to data
quiz.e: A model can achieve strong average performance while systematically failing a minority subgroup, which is why fairness requires checking outcomes across groups, not just an aggregate score.

quiz.q: What does 'accountability' mean in AI ethics?
o: A person or organization is responsible for harm caused by an AI system, not the algorithm itself
Only the end user can be blamed for AI errors
AI systems are legally considered independent entities
Accountability only applies to open-source AI projects
quiz.e: Accountability places responsibility for an AI system's real-world impact on the people and organizations who built and deployed it — 'the algorithm did it' isn't a valid excuse.

quiz.q: Why is explainability especially important in domains like healthcare or criminal justice?
o: Because wrong or opaque decisions in these domains have serious, high-stakes consequences for real people
Because explainability makes models run faster
Because these fields never use AI systems
Because explainable models are always more accurate
quiz.e: In high-stakes decisions affecting health, freedom, or finances, being able to explain why an AI reached a conclusion is critical for trust, correction, and due process.

quiz.q: What ethical concern is most directly raised by deepfake technology?
o: Consent, misinformation, and erosion of trust in audio/video evidence
Increased computing costs for video storage
quiz.e: Deepfakes can fabricate convincing but false depictions of real people, raising serious concerns about consent, spreading misinformation, and undermining trust in recorded media.

quiz.q: Why do AI systems trained on large personal datasets raise privacy concerns?
o: Because the data may have been collected without full user awareness or consent
Because AI systems never use personal data
Because personal data cannot legally be stored digitally
Because training always deletes the underlying data afterward
quiz.e: Many AI systems are trained on massive datasets scraped or collected in ways users may not have been fully informed about, raising consent and privacy issues.

quiz.q: What does copyright protect, and when does that protection begin?
o: Original creative or technical work, protected automatically the moment it is created
Only inventions, and only after a government application is approved
Nothing until a formal registration fee is paid
Only works published in physical print
quiz.e: Copyright applies automatically upon creation of an original work (including code), giving the creator exclusive rights without needing to file anything, unlike a patent.

quiz.q: How does a patent differ from copyright?
o: A patent protects a novel invention or process and requires formal application/approval, while copyright protects creative expression automatically
A patent and copyright are two names for the same legal protection
Copyright requires a formal government application, but a patent does not
Patents only apply to open-source software
quiz.e: Patents cover inventions/processes and require applying to a patent office, while copyright covers original expression (including code) and attaches automatically at creation.

quiz.q: What is the key feature of a permissive open-source license like MIT?
o: It allows broad reuse, even in closed-source commercial products, typically requiring only attribution
It requires all derivative works to also be open source
It prohibits any commercial use whatsoever
It only applies to code written in Python
quiz.e: Permissive licenses like MIT or Apache impose minimal restrictions — usually just keeping the original attribution — even when the code is used in proprietary software.

quiz.q: What is the defining feature of a copyleft license like the GPL?
o: Any derivative work using the code must also be released under the same open license
It grants no rights to use the code at all
It expires automatically after one year
It only applies to hardware designs
quiz.e: Copyleft licenses like the GPL require that anything built using the licensed code be distributed under the same license terms, which is why they're sometimes called 'viral.'

quiz.q: What legal risk can arise from including GPL-licensed code in a closed-source commercial product?
o: None — GPL code can always be used freely in any product
It can create real legal liability, since GPL requires derivative works to also be open-sourced
It automatically converts the entire company to a nonprofit
It only affects the original GPL license holder, not the company using it
quiz.e: Shipping GPL-licensed code inside closed-source software violates the license's copyleft terms and can expose the company to legal liability.

quiz.q: What primarily distinguishes a front-end developer's work from a back-end developer's?
o: Front-end focuses on the user-facing interface; back-end focuses on servers, databases, and APIs
Front-end developers never write any code
Back-end developers only design visual layouts
There is no meaningful difference between the two roles
quiz.e: Front-end work centers on what users see and interact with directly, while back-end work builds the underlying logic, data storage, and services that power it.

quiz.q: What does a data scientist typically do?
o: Extract insights and build predictive models from data using statistics and programming
Only design the visual appearance of a website
Manage a company's physical server hardware exclusively
Write legal contracts for software licensing
quiz.e: Data scientists combine statistics, programming (often Python or SQL), and visualization to find patterns and build models from data.

quiz.q: What is the primary focus of a UX/UI designer's role?
o: How usable and intuitive a product feels, blending research and visual design
Writing the back-end database queries for an application
Filing patents for a company's inventions
quiz.e: UX/UI design centers on usability and user experience — informed by research and psychology — rather than on writing the underlying production code.

quiz.q: What is a penetration tester hired to do?
o: Deliberately attempt to break into systems to find vulnerabilities before real attackers do
quiz.e: Penetration testers simulate real attacks on a system with permission, uncovering security weaknesses so they can be fixed proactively.

quiz.q: Which statement about entering the tech industry is most accurate?
o: A four-year degree is the only legitimate path into a tech career
Bootcamps, certifications, self-teaching, and project portfolios are all recognized alternative paths alongside a degree
Only self-taught programmers can become software engineers
Tech careers require no demonstrable skills, only a diploma
quiz.e: The tech industry recognizes multiple valid entry paths, and many employers weigh demonstrated skills and portfolios alongside or instead of formal degrees.

quiz.q: A city deploys a predictive policing tool that sends more patrols to a neighborhood based on past arrest data, which then leads to more arrests there, reinforcing the pattern. What does this best illustrate?
o: A feedback loop amplifying algorithmic bias
quiz.e: This is a classic feedback loop: biased historical data drives biased action, which generates new data that appears to confirm and reinforce the original bias.

quiz.q: A facial recognition system performs significantly worse on darker-skinned faces because its training set was overwhelmingly composed of lighter-skinned faces. What is this an example of?
o: Bias from underrepresentation in training data
An intentional design goal of the system
quiz.e: When a dataset underrepresents certain groups, the resulting model tends to perform worse for those groups — a common and well-documented source of algorithmic bias.

quiz.q: A company blames 'the algorithm' when its automated loan-approval system unfairly denies qualified applicants from a certain group. Why is this response ethically inadequate?
o: Accountability requires that the people/organization behind the system take responsibility, not the algorithm itself
The algorithm is legally a separate entity that can be sued directly
Loan approval systems are not covered by AI ethics
This response is fully adequate and requires no follow-up
quiz.e: In AI ethics, responsibility for an automated system's harms lies with the humans and organization who built, deployed, and maintained it — not with the software itself.

quiz.q: A developer copies a large chunk of GPL-licensed code into their proprietary, closed-source app without releasing their source. What is the issue?
o: This likely violates the GPL's copyleft requirement that derivative works also be open-sourced
There is no issue since all code online is free to use however you want
This is only a problem if the original author never distributed the code
GPL only applies to hardware, not software
quiz.e: The GPL is a copyleft license: using its code in a derivative work generally requires releasing that derivative under the same license, so closed-sourcing it breaches the terms.

quiz.q: A student says an AI chatbot 'decided' to give biased advice, so no person is at fault. Why does this reasoning fail under standard AI ethics principles?
o: Accountability holds the people/organization who built and deployed the system responsible for its outputs
AI systems are legally autonomous decision-makers with no human oversight
Bias in chatbots is always intentional and therefore blameless
This reasoning is correct and reflects the accepted standard
quiz.e: AI ethics rejects treating the system as an autonomous, blameless actor; responsibility traces back to the humans and organizations who designed, trained, and deployed it.

quiz.q: Which pairing correctly matches a role to its primary responsibility?
o: DevOps engineer — manages deployment pipelines and infrastructure reliability
UX/UI designer — writes back-end database queries
Data scientist — designs a company's network firewall
Front-end developer — files patents for company inventions
quiz.e: DevOps engineers focus on deployment automation, infrastructure, and keeping systems running reliably — the other pairings mismatch role and responsibility.

quiz.q: Why is 'can we build this AI system' a different kind of question from 'should we build this AI system'?
o: The first is a technical feasibility question; the second is an ethical judgment about consequences and values
They are exactly the same question phrased differently
Only the first question is ever relevant in engineering
AI ethics only concerns itself with technical feasibility
quiz.e: Technical feasibility and ethical appropriateness are separate axes of evaluation — a system can be technically buildable while still raising serious ethical concerns about whether it should be built or deployed.

quiz.q: A photo-sharing app scrapes millions of public photos without notifying the people in them to train a facial recognition model. What is the primary ethical issue?
o: Lack of informed consent from the people whose images were used
The photos were technically difficult to download
The model will definitely have 100% accuracy
There is no ethical issue since the photos were publicly visible
quiz.e: Public visibility of a photo does not equal consent to have it used for training a facial recognition model — the core issue is the lack of informed consent from those depicted.

quiz.q: Why might using someone else's code found online without checking its license create legal risk?
o: Different licenses impose different obligations, and violating them (e.g. missing attribution or closed-sourcing copyleft code) can lead to liability
All code found online is automatically public domain
Licenses are only suggestions with no legal weight
Checking a license is only necessary for patented inventions
quiz.e: Every open-source license carries specific legal terms; ignoring them and not verifying compliance can expose a project or company to real legal consequences.

flashcards.d: The smallest unit of digital data, representing either a 0 or a 1.
A group of 8 bits, commonly used as the basic unit of storage size.
A base-2 number system using only the digits 0 and 1, used internally by all digital computers.
A base-16 number system using digits 0-9 and letters A-F; each hex digit represents exactly 4 bits.
Volatile, fast working memory that temporarily holds data and programs currently in use; contents are lost when power is off.
The hardware component that fetches, decodes, and executes program instructions; often called the computer's 'brain.'
System software that manages hardware resources (memory, CPU, storage) and provides a platform for running applications.
A character encoding standard that assigns a numeric value to each English letter, digit, and common symbol.
A character encoding standard that extends ASCII to represent text from virtually all the world's languages and symbols.
Storage, such as an SSD or hard drive, that retains its data even when the power is turned off.
A named storage location in a program that holds a value, which can be changed while the program runs.
A classification (such as integer, float, string, or boolean) that determines what kind of value a variable holds and what operations are valid on it.
An error that occurs when code does not follow the grammatical rules of the programming language, preventing it from running.
A bug where code runs without crashing but produces an incorrect result due to a flaw in the reasoning or algorithm.
An error that occurs while a program is executing, such as dividing by zero or accessing a missing file.
A program that translates entire source code into machine code before the program is run.
A program that translates and executes source code line-by-line, without producing a separate machine-code file first.
The operation of joining two or more strings together into one, often using the + operator.
A data type with only two possible values: true or false.
A named, reusable block of code that performs a specific task and can be called multiple times from a program.
A control structure that executes a block of code only when a specified boolean condition is true.
A loop structure typically used to repeat code a known or fixed number of times, often iterating over a range or collection.
A loop structure that repeats a block of code as long as a specified condition remains true.
A reusable, named block of code that performs a specific task and can accept inputs (parameters) and return a value.
A parameter is the placeholder variable in a function's definition; an argument is the actual value passed in when the function is called.
A statement that sends a value back to the code that called a function and immediately ends that function's execution.
The region of a program where a particular variable can be accessed, such as local (inside a function) or global (throughout the program).
A technique where a function calls itself to solve smaller instances of the same problem, requiring a base case to stop.
A loop whose stopping condition never becomes false, causing it to repeat forever unless forcibly stopped.
The condition in a recursive function that stops further recursive calls, preventing infinite recursion.
An ordered collection of elements, each accessible by a numeric index, typically starting at 0.
A LIFO (Last In, First Out) data structure where elements are added and removed from the same end (the top), via push and pop.
A FIFO (First In, First Out) data structure where elements are added at the back (enqueue) and removed from the front (dequeue).
A data structure that stores key-value pairs, allowing fast lookup of a value using its unique key.
A collection that stores only unique values, with no duplicates, supporting operations like union and intersection.
A hierarchical data structure of nodes connected by edges, starting from a single root node, with no cycles.
A structure consisting of nodes (vertices) connected by edges, which may be directed or undirected, used to model networks and relationships.
The process of converting a key into an index using a hash function, enabling fast data lookup in a hash map.
The topmost node in a tree, from which all other nodes descend; it has no parent.
A node in a tree that has no children, located at the end of a branch.
A precise, finite, step-by-step procedure for solving a problem or completing a task.
A search algorithm that checks each element of a collection one at a time until the target is found or the end is reached; runs in O(n) time.
A search algorithm that repeatedly halves a sorted collection to locate a target value; runs in O(log n) time but requires sorted data.
A mathematical notation used to describe how an algorithm's runtime or memory usage grows as the size of its input increases.
A growth rate where runtime increases with the square of the input size, often caused by nested loops over the same data, as in bubble sort.
A growth rate where runtime increases very slowly as input grows, typical of algorithms that repeatedly halve the problem, like binary search.
A simple sorting algorithm that repeatedly compares and swaps adjacent out-of-order elements; runs in O(n²) time.
A divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm that splits data in half, recursively sorts each half, and merges the results; more efficient than bubble sort for large data.
An informal, human-readable description of an algorithm's steps, used for planning before writing actual code.
A problem-solving strategy of breaking a large, complex problem into smaller, more manageable subproblems.
A global network of interconnected computer networks that communicate using standardized protocols.
A system of linked documents (webpages) accessed via the internet, using HTTP/HTTPS and URLs.
A unique numeric label assigned to a device on a network, used to identify and locate it for data transmission.
A system that translates human-readable domain names (like example.com) into numeric IP addresses.
HTTP is the protocol used for communication between web browsers and servers; HTTPS is its encrypted, secure version.
A Uniform Resource Locator specifying the address of a resource on the internet, including protocol, domain, and path.
A structure where a client (e.g., a browser) requests resources or services from a server, which stores and provides them.
A three-digit code returned by a server indicating the result of a request, such as 200 (OK), 404 (Not Found), or 500 (Server Error).
A small unit of data that is transmitted across a network and reassembled with other packets at its destination.
The process of scrambling data so that only someone with the correct key can read it, protecting data in transit or storage.
The process of converting readable data (plaintext) into unreadable form (ciphertext) using a key, reversible only by someone with the correct key.
Encryption that uses the same key to both encrypt and decrypt data; fast, but requires securely sharing the key.
Encryption using a public key to encrypt and a mathematically linked private key to decrypt, allowing the public key to be shared openly.
A one-way function that converts data into a fixed-length string; used to verify passwords or file integrity, but cannot be reversed.
An incident where unauthorized parties access sensitive stored data, often via stolen credentials, phishing, or unpatched software.
A security method requiring two forms of proof (like a password plus a code sent to your phone) before granting access.
A small piece of data a website stores in your browser to remember information like login state or preferences between visits.
A cookie set by a domain other than the one you're visiting, commonly used by advertisers to track browsing across multiple sites.
The EU's General Data Protection Regulation, which grants individuals rights over their personal data and requires organizations to handle it responsibly.
A GDPR right allowing individuals to request that a company delete their personal data ("right to be forgotten").
A social engineering attack that tricks users into revealing credentials or installing malware by impersonating a trusted source.
Malicious software designed to damage, disrupt, or gain unauthorized access to a system, including viruses, worms, and ransomware.
Malware that encrypts a victim's files and demands payment in exchange for the decryption key.
A system that filters network traffic based on security rules, blocking unauthorized access while permitting legitimate traffic.
A security practice of giving users and programs only the minimum access necessary to perform their function.
Manipulating people (rather than exploiting technical flaws) into giving up confidential information or access.
The privacy principle of collecting only the personal data actually needed for a specific, stated purpose.
An attack where stolen username/password pairs from one breach are tried on other sites, exploiting password reuse.
Adding random data to a password before hashing it, so identical passwords produce different hashes and are harder to crack in bulk.
A tracking technique that identifies a browser/device by its unique combination of settings and hardware traits, used as third-party cookies decline.
Systematically unfair outcomes produced by a computer system for certain groups, usually caused by biased training data or flawed model design.
A feature that indirectly encodes a sensitive attribute (like race) through correlation, such as zip code, even when that attribute is excluded from a dataset.
A cycle where a biased model's outputs generate new data that reinforces and amplifies the original bias over time.
A situation where a policy or algorithm that appears neutral produces significantly worse outcomes for one group compared to others.
The degree to which people can understand how and why an AI system reached a particular decision.
The ability to describe, in human-understandable terms, why an AI model produced a specific output — critical in high-stakes decisions.
The principle that a person or organization, not the algorithm itself, bears responsibility when an AI system causes harm.
AI-generated audio or video that convincingly fabricates a person saying or doing something they never actually did.
Legal protection that automatically applies to original creative or technical work, giving the creator exclusive rights to copy, modify, and distribute it.
Legal protection for a novel invention or process, granted for a limited time after formal application, preventing others from using it without permission.
A license that grants others legal permission to use, modify, and share source code, under conditions the license specifies.
An open-source license (e.g. MIT, Apache) allowing broad reuse, including in closed-source products, typically requiring only attribution.
An open-source license (e.g. GPL) requiring that derivative works built on the code also be released under the same open license.
A software engineer who builds the user-facing part of an application: layout, interactivity, and visual presentation.
A software engineer who builds the server-side logic, databases, and APIs that power an application behind the scenes.
A professional who extracts insights and builds predictive models from data using statistics, programming, and visualization.
A professional who designs how usable, intuitive, and visually coherent a product feels, blending research and visual design.
A professional who manages the deployment pipeline and infrastructure that keeps software running reliably in production.
A cybersecurity professional hired to deliberately attempt to break into systems, finding vulnerabilities before real attackers do.
An intensive, short-term training program (often a few months) designed to teach practical programming skills as an alternative to a traditional degree.

PART_A.q: How many distinct values can a single byte (8 bits) represent?
PART_A.e: A byte has 8 bits, and 2^8 = 256 distinct values, ranging from 0 to 255.

PART_A.q: What does binary 1011 equal in decimal?
How many bits does one hexadecimal digit represent?
PART_A.e: One hex digit (0-9, A-F) maps exactly to a 4-bit nibble.

PART_A.q: Which component fetches, decodes, and executes instructions?
PART_A.e: The CPU is the central processing unit that carries out the fetch-decode-execute cycle.

PART_A.q: Which type of memory is erased when the power is turned off?
PART_A.e: RAM (main memory) is volatile and loses its contents without power, unlike permanent storage.

PART_A.q: In programming, what is a variable?
o: A fixed value that never changes
A named location that stores a value which can change
PART_A.e: A variable is a named storage location whose value can be changed as the program runs.

PART_A.q: What is the purpose of debugging?
o: Finding and fixing errors in code
PART_A.e: Debugging is the process of locating and correcting errors (bugs) in a program.

PART_A.q: Which of the following is an example of an operator?
PART_A.e: + is an arithmetic operator used to combine or compute values in an expression.

PART_A.q: What distinguishes a compiled language from an interpreted one?
o: Compiled code is translated to machine code before running; interpreted code is executed line by line
PART_A.e: Compiled languages are translated ahead of time into machine code, while interpreted languages are executed statement by statement at runtime.

PART_A.q: What does a for loop typically use to control repetition?
PART_A.e: For loops usually rely on a counter variable that tracks the number of iterations.

PART_A.q: What is 'scope' in programming?
o: The region of code where a variable can be accessed
The number of functions in a program
PART_A.e: Scope defines where in the code a variable name is valid and accessible.

PART_A.q: Which control structure executes a block of code only if a condition is true?
PART_A.e: An if statement (conditional) runs its block only when its condition evaluates to true.

PART_A.q: What is a function parameter?
o: A value passed into a function when it is called
PART_A.e: A parameter is a placeholder variable that receives the value passed into a function at call time.

PART_A.q: Which data structure follows Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) order?
PART_A.e: A stack removes the most recently added item first, which is the LIFO principle.

PART_A.q: Which data structure follows First-In-First-Out (FIFO) order?
PART_A.e: A queue processes items in the order they were added, removing the oldest item first (FIFO).

PART_A.q: What is a key feature of a set data structure?
o: It maintains insertion order strictly like a queue
PART_A.e: Sets are defined by storing only unique elements, with no duplicates allowed.

PART_A.q: What do dictionaries (hash maps) use to quickly locate values?
PART_A.e: Dictionaries map unique keys to values, allowing fast lookup by key.

PART_A.q: What is an algorithm?
o: A step-by-step procedure for solving a problem
PART_A.e: An algorithm is a well-defined sequence of steps used to solve a problem or complete a task.

PART_A.q: What does Big-O notation describe?
o: The exact runtime of a program in seconds
How an algorithm's time or space needs grow as input size increases
The number of bugs in code
PART_A.e: Big-O notation describes the growth rate of an algorithm's resource use as the input size grows, not exact timing.

PART_A.q: Which search algorithm requires the data to be sorted first?
PART_A.e: Binary search repeatedly halves a sorted range, which only works correctly on sorted data.

PART_A.q: What is the Big-O time complexity of linear search in the worst case?
PART_A.e: Linear search may need to check every element once, giving worst-case O(n) time.

PART_A.q: What translates a human-readable domain name into an IP address?
PART_A.e: DNS (Domain Name System) resolves domain names into the numeric IP addresses computers use to connect.

PART_A.q: Which HTTP status code range indicates a successful response?
PART_A.e: HTTP status codes in the 200s (e.g., 200 OK) indicate the request succeeded.

PART_A.q: What is the key difference between the Internet and the Web?
o: They are exactly the same thing
The Internet is the physical/network infrastructure; the Web is a service (pages/hyperlinks) that runs on top of it
The Web existed before the Internet
PART_A.e: The Internet is the underlying global network infrastructure, while the Web (HTTP, HTML, hyperlinks) is one application that runs over that infrastructure.

PART_A.q: What does HTTPS add to standard HTTP communication?
PART_A.e: HTTPS adds TLS/SSL encryption on top of HTTP, protecting data from being read or tampered with in transit.

PART_A.q: What does encryption do to data?
o: Scrambles it so only authorized parties with the key can read it
PART_A.e: Encryption transforms readable data into unreadable ciphertext that can only be decoded with the correct key.

PART_A.q: What is a data breach?
o: An incident where sensitive data is accessed or exposed without authorization
PART_A.e: A data breach occurs when protected or sensitive data is accessed, stolen, or exposed without permission.

PART_A.q: What is the primary purpose of cookies in web browsing?
o: To store small pieces of data that let websites remember information across visits
PART_A.e: Cookies are small files websites use to store data such as login state or preferences between visits, and are also used for tracking.

PART_A.q: What is algorithmic bias?
o: A bug that crashes a program
When an algorithm produces systematically unfair outcomes for certain groups due to skewed data or design
PART_A.e: Algorithmic bias occurs when an algorithm's outputs unfairly disadvantage particular groups, often due to biased training data or design choices.

PART_A.q: What does a software license typically govern?
o: The color of the user interface
How the software may be legally used, copied, modified, or distributed
PART_A.e: A license is a legal agreement specifying the terms under which software can be used, copied, modified, or shared.

PART_B1.q: A computer's storage (SSD/hard drive) differs from RAM primarily because storage is:
PART_B1.e: Storage is non-volatile, retaining data even when power is removed, unlike RAM which is volatile.

PART_B1.q: What is the decimal value of the binary number 1111?
Which of these is considered good practice for writing readable code?
o: Using descriptive variable names and consistent formatting
Writing the whole program as one line
PART_B1.e: Readable code uses clear, descriptive names and consistent style so others (and future you) can understand it easily.

PART_B1.q: What is a syntax error?
o: An error caused by faulty logic that gives wrong results
A violation of a programming language's grammar rules that prevents the code from running
PART_B1.e: A syntax error occurs when code doesn't follow the rules of the language's grammar, so it fails to parse or compile.

PART_B1.q: What happens to a variable declared inside a function once the function finishes running (assuming it is a local variable)?
o: It goes out of scope and is no longer accessible
PART_B1.e: Local variables exist only within the function's scope and are discarded once the function returns.

PART_B1.q: Which loop type is best suited when the number of iterations is not known in advance and depends on a condition?
o: For loop with a fixed range
PART_B1.e: A while loop continues as long as its condition holds, making it ideal when the iteration count isn't known ahead of time.

PART_B1.q: Which data structure would be most appropriate for representing a family tree with parent-child relationships?
PART_B1.e: A tree naturally models hierarchical parent-child relationships like a family tree or org chart.

PART_B1.q: An array differs from a linked list in that an array typically provides:
o: Slower access to elements by index
Constant-time (O(1)) access to any element by its index
No way to store multiple values
PART_B1.e: Arrays store elements in contiguous memory, allowing direct O(1) indexed access, unlike linked lists which require traversal.

PART_B1.q: Which sorting algorithm repeatedly swaps adjacent elements that are out of order?
PART_B1.e: Bubble sort repeatedly steps through the list, swapping adjacent elements that are in the wrong order.

PART_B1.q: An algorithm with time complexity O(n^2) compared to one with O(n log n) will generally, for large inputs:
o: Run at exactly the same speed
PART_B1.e: O(n^2) grows faster than O(n log n) as input size increases, so it becomes slower for large inputs.

PART_B1.q: What does a web browser do first when you type a URL, before it can request the page?
o: Look up the domain's IP address via DNS
PART_B1.e: The browser must resolve the domain name to an IP address via DNS before it can send an HTTP request to the server.

PART_B1.q: Which HTTP status code indicates that a requested resource was not found?
PART_B1.e: 404 Not Found is the standard status code for a resource that does not exist on the server.

PART_B1.q: Which of these best describes the goal of GDPR-style privacy regulations?
o: To ban all data collection entirely
To give individuals rights over their personal data and require organizations to handle it responsibly
To eliminate the need for passwords
PART_B1.e: GDPR-style regulations grant individuals rights over their personal data and impose responsible data-handling obligations on organizations.

PART_B1.q: What is a firewall used for in cybersecurity?
o: Monitoring and controlling incoming/outgoing network traffic based on security rules
PART_B1.e: A firewall filters network traffic according to defined security rules to block unauthorized access.

PART_B1.q: Why is transparency often recommended when deploying AI systems that affect people's lives?
o: It makes the AI run faster
It helps people understand and challenge decisions, reducing hidden bias and unfairness
PART_B1.e: Transparency allows people to understand how AI decisions are made, enabling accountability and the ability to contest unfair outcomes.

PART_B1.q: What is the purpose of an 'else' clause when paired with an 'if' statement?
o: To repeat a block of code
To run a block of code when the if condition is false
PART_B1.e: The else clause provides an alternative block of code to run when the associated if condition evaluates to false.

PART_B1.q: What is a common pitfall when using loops?
o: An off-by-one error causing the loop to run one time too many or too few
PART_B1.e: Off-by-one errors, where a loop iterates one time too many or too few, are among the most common loop bugs.

PART_B1.q: Which is true of a hash map (dictionary)'s average-case lookup time?
PART_B1.e: Hash maps use a hash function to place data, giving average-case O(1) lookup time.

PART_B1.q: What is the main goal of a divide-and-conquer problem-solving strategy?
o: Solve the entire problem at once with no breakdown
Break a problem into smaller subproblems, solve them, and combine results
PART_B1.e: Divide-and-conquer splits a large problem into smaller, more manageable subproblems, solves each, then merges the results.

PART_B1.q: What does an IP address uniquely identify on a network?
o: A device's location/address for sending and receiving data
PART_B1.e: An IP address uniquely identifies a device on a network so data can be routed to and from it.

PART_B2.q: Why do computers use binary instead of decimal internally?
o: Binary is easier for humans to read
Transistors are simplest to build as two-state (on/off) switches
Binary uses fewer digits so it's always faster to compute
Decimal is not a real number system
PART_B2.e: Binary maps naturally onto transistors' two stable states (on/off), making it the simplest and most reliable system for digital hardware.

PART_B2.q: Which of the following is an example of a runtime error rather than a syntax error?
o: Dividing a number by zero while the program is running
PART_B2.e: A runtime error, such as division by zero, occurs while the program is executing correctly-formed code, unlike a syntax error caught before execution.

PART_B2.q: In a function, what is the difference between a parameter and an argument?
o: They are exactly the same with no difference
A parameter is the placeholder in the function definition; an argument is the actual value passed in when calling it
An argument is only used in loops
A parameter can only be a number
PART_B2.e: Parameters are the named placeholders in a function's definition, while arguments are the actual values supplied at the call site.

PART_B2.q: When should you prefer a queue over a stack?
o: When you need Last-In-First-Out processing, like undo history
When you need First-In-First-Out processing, like a print job or task queue
When you need to store only unique values
When you need constant-time indexed access
PART_B2.e: A queue is appropriate when items must be processed in the order they arrived (FIFO), such as tasks waiting in line.

PART_B2.q: Which best describes a greedy algorithm strategy?
o: It always finds the optimal solution to every problem
It makes the locally best choice at each step, hoping to reach a good overall solution
It tries every possible combination exhaustively
It only works on sorted arrays
PART_B2.e: Greedy algorithms make the best-looking choice at each step without reconsidering, which is fast but doesn't guarantee a global optimum for every problem.

PART_B2.q: What role does a web server play when a browser requests a page?
o: It receives the HTTP request and sends back a response, such as an HTML page
It converts domain names into hexadecimal
It replaces the need for the Internet
PART_B2.e: A web server listens for HTTP requests and responds with the requested resource, such as an HTML document.

PART_B2.q: Why are strong, unique passwords considered a cybersecurity fundamental?
o: They make the computer run faster
They reduce the risk of accounts being compromised through guessing or reused-credential attacks
They are required by every programming language
They automatically encrypt all files on a device
PART_B2.e: Strong, unique passwords make it much harder for attackers to guess credentials or exploit reused passwords from other breaches.

PART_B2.q: Which of these best exemplifies a career path directly tied to building software systems?
PART_B2.e: A software engineer designs, builds, and maintains software systems, making it a direct tech career path covered in this unit.

PART_B2.q: What is a key trade-off when choosing between an array and a linked list for frequent insertions in the middle of the collection?
o: Arrays always insert faster in the middle
Linked lists can insert in the middle more efficiently since no shifting of elements is needed
Both have identical performance in every case
PART_B2.e: Linked lists allow O(1) insertion at a known position by just relinking pointers, while arrays must shift subsequent elements, which is slower.

PART_B2.q: What is the purpose of a status code like 500 in an HTTP response?
o: It indicates the request succeeded perfectly
It indicates a server-side error occurred while processing the request
It means the page was redirected
It means the user is not authenticated
PART_B2.e: A 500 status code signals an internal server error, meaning something went wrong on the server while handling the request.

PART_C.q: Written response: choose TWO concepts from different units and construct an argument connecting them. Cite specific evidence from each.
o: Names both concepts precisely, gives concrete evidence for each, and explains the causal/logical bridge
Lists the two topics without connecting them
Describes only one concept in detail
Gives a personal opinion with no course evidence
PART_C.e: Strong responses anchor every claim in specific unit content.

PART_C.q: Essay plan: identify the single most important takeaway of this course. Defend it using three units as evidence, then address one counterargument.
o: Clear thesis, three unit-specific pieces of evidence, genuine counterargument, resolution
PART_C.e: Full argumentative architecture earns top marks.
